editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "“光的艺术”于 2026 年 11 月 20 日至 29 日将南非灯光装置艺术带到开普敦诺瓦尔基金会的庭园中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/0992678_0-1030x343.webp", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "随着开普敦的日光消散，诺瓦尔基金会的庭园将成为与光线、空间及自然环境进行艺术邂逅的场所。“光的艺术”将 LUMENOCITY 的精选装置艺术带到托凯，让访客有机会在全新的环境中体验南非艺术家的作品。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些装置艺术走出了原本的城市语境，在树木、草坪和盘旋的小径间呈现，邀请观众思考光线如何重塑熟悉的景观并改变我们对空间的感知。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“光的艺术”并非一场传统的画廊展览，而是一次户外的旅程。访客可以按照自己的节奏探索这些点亮的装置，整个体验大约需要 60 至 90 分钟。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这次展出提供了一个在博物馆室内空间之外接触当代艺术实践的机会，在这里，艺术品、环境与观众之间的关系成为了体验的核心。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该活动老少咸宜，现场还将设有餐车和茶点，打造一个老少咸宜且轻松的艺术探索之夜。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该活动将于 2026 年 11 月 20 日至 29 日在托凯的诺瓦尔基金会举行，11 月 23 日和 24 日除外。", "links": [{"text": "Norval Foundation", "url": "https://www.theartoflight.co.za/"}], "translated": true}]

article_text:
The Art of Light brings South African light installations to the gardens of Norval Foundation in Cape Town, from 20 to 29 November 2026.

As daylight fades over Cape Town, the gardens of Norval Foundation will become a setting for artistic encounters with light, space and the natural environment. ‘The Art of Light’ brings a selection of installations from LUMENOCITY to Tokai, giving visitors the chance to experience works by South African artists in a new setting.

Moving beyond their original urban context, the installations will be presented among trees, lawns and winding pathways, inviting audiences to consider how light transforms familiar landscapes and alters our perception of space.

Rather than a conventional gallery exhibition, ‘The Art of Light’ unfolds as an outdoor journey. Visitors can explore the illuminated installations at their own pace, with the experience taking approximately 60 to 90 minutes.

The presentation offers an opportunity to encounter contemporary artistic practices beyond the museum’s interior, where the relationship between artwork, environment and audience becomes central to the experience.

Suitable for all ages, the event will also feature food trucks and refreshments, creating an accessible evening of art and exploration.

This event will take place at the Norval Foundation in Tokai, from 20 to 29 November 2026, excluding 23 and 24 November.

title_original: First Trailer for Greta Gerwig’s Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew Imagines a Fantastical World
editorial_title_zh: 格蕾塔·葛韦格执导的《纳尼亚传奇：魔法师的外甥》首支预告片展现奇幻世界
editorial_excerpt_zh: 在执导了制片厂大片《芭比》之后，格蕾塔·葛韦格转投Netflix，执导了《纳尼亚传奇：魔法师的外甥》的改编电影。该片将获得相当长的院线公映期，于2027年2月12日在IMAX及全球影院上映，随后于…在Netflix上线
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "在执导了制片厂大片《芭比》之后，格蕾塔·葛韦格转投Netflix，执导了《纳尼亚传奇：魔法师的外甥》的改编电影。该片将获得相当长的院线公映期，于2027年2月12日在IMAX及全球影院上映，随后于2027年4月2日在Netflix上线——这一院线窗口期比一些传统制片厂在将电影投放到SVOD平台之前所采用的还要长。她对C·S·刘易斯作品的改编集结了大卫·麦肯纳、比阿特丽斯·坎贝尔、艾玛·麦基、凯瑞·穆里根、塞亚斯·希恩斯、丹尼尔·克雷格和梅丽尔·斯特里普，由齐柏林飞艇乐队（Led Zeppelin）配乐的首支预告片现已发布。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“当我第一次读到《魔法师的外甥》时我还只是个孩子，我爱上了那只宇宙雄狮用歌声唱出纳尼亚世界的华丽而不可思议、却又极其出色的构思，”葛韦格说道。“我当时并不知道自己长大后会拍电影，但一个由音乐构筑的宇宙这个想法一直留在我心中。受邀将其具象化是我一生的荣幸。因为C·S·刘易斯的《纳尼亚传奇》，我相信了魔法、隐藏的世界和冒险。我相信任何地方都可以充满魔力，任何人都可能被卷入史诗之中。那种惊奇与敬畏感对所有人都是开放的，甚至是像我这样普通的人……它改变了我。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "请观看由西莫斯·迈克加维（《爱欲将死》、《夜行动物》、《安娜·卡列尼娜》）摄影的电影预告片和海报：", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Narnia-poster-960x1200.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Following her studio blockbuster Barbie , Greta Gerwig hopped over to Netflix to direct an adaptation of Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew , which will get quite the lengthy theatrical run, kicking off in IMAX and global theaters on February 12, 2027, followed by a Netflix debut on April 2, 2027––a longer theatrical window than some legacy studios manage before dropping their films on SVOD. Her C.S. Lewis adaptation stars David McKenna, Beatrice Campbell, Emma Mackey, Carey Mulligan, Ciarán Hinds, Daniel Craig, and Meryl Streep, and the first, Led Zeppelin-scored trailer has arrived.

“I was a child when I first read The Magician’s Nephew , and I fell in love with the gorgeously improbable but completely brilliant concept of a cosmic lion singing the world of Narnia to life,” says Gerwig. “I didn’t know that I would grow up to make films, but a universe built out of music is an idea that always lived in my heart. It is the honor of a lifetime to be asked to imagine it into being. Because of C. S. Lewis’s The Chronicles of Narnia , I believed in magic and hidden worlds and adventure. I believed that anywhere could be enchanted and that anyone could be swept up into an epic. That wonder and awe was available to everyone, even ordinary people like me…It transformed me.”

title_original: ‘You can’t make this stuff up’: why we remain fascinated by Elizabeth Holmes
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "D avid Agus’s first encounter with Elizabeth Holmes at a health conference came as a shock. The Holmes he met in the green room was personable and pleasant. The Holmes he interviewed on stage was altogether different.", "links": [{"text": "Elizabeth Holmes", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/elizabeth-holmes"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“The accent changed: this deep voice, very serious,” Agus, a medical oncologist , recalls by phone from Los Angeles. “It was as if I had met a person and then interviewed a separate person. That transition from the green room to the stage – I had never experienced something like that before.”", "links": [{"text": "Agus, a medical oncologist", "url": "https://davidagus.com/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Holmes is not like you or me. She was still a teenager when she founded Theranos, touting technology capable of performing medical tests using only a few drops of blood. She cultivated a distinctive persona: blond hair, an unblinking gaze, a husky voice and a black turtleneck worn in homage to Apple co-founder Steve Jobs .", "links": [{"text": "Steve Jobs", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/technology/stevejobs"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Holmes mesmerised investors and board members including Rupert Murdoch, Larry Ellison, Carlos Slim and former secretaries of state Henry Kissinger and George Shultz. She became America’s youngest self-made female billionaire. But it was all an illusion, a confidence trick built on a scam. Holmes’s shining career ended in disgrace and imprisonment.", "links": [{"text": "Henry Kissinger", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/global/2023/nov/29/henry-kissinger-obituary"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Margaret O’Mara , a history professor at the University of Washington in Seattle and author of The Code: Silicon Valley and the Remaking of America, says: “You can’t make this stuff up. If some screenwriter had tried to manufacture this out of whole cloth people would be like, no, this is an unbelievable story. Yet it’s real. Who’s the real Elizabeth Holmes? That’s a question that still hasn’t been answered .”", "links": [{"text": "Margaret O’Mara", "url": "https://history.washington.edu/people/margaret-omara"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Perhaps the answer lies in You Can See Everything , a reality-bending documentary, released in the US on Friday, in which Holmes goes eyeball-to-eyeball with the absurdist comedian Nathan Fielder, who directs along with Lance Oppenheim. It was filmed in the 34 days before she was due to report to federal prison camp Bryan in Texas to begin her 11-year sentence for wire fraud and conspiracy.", "links": [{"text": "You Can See Everything", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oct/01/you-can-see-everything-movie-review"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That fate seemed unthinkable in 2003 when, at the age of 19, Holmes dropped out of Stanford University and established Theranos , promising to revolutionise the multibillion-dollar blood-testing industry by using microfluidics to run hundreds of tests on just a few drops of blood.", "links": [{"text": "Theranos", "url": "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theranos"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "She found a receptive audience among investors who wanted Silicon Valley to deliver more than Facebook friends. O’Mara explains: “ She stands out in her ascent as a female entrepreneur at a time when men were dominating the scene and she was doing something that was in tech but seemed to be change-the-world-tech.", "links": [{"text": "Silicon Valley", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/technology/silicon-valley"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“The techlash wasn’t brewing yet but, where there was criticism of Silicon Valley, it was like: ‘Hey, you’ve got all these brilliant people and all you’re doing is building apps? Why don’t you do something a little more meaningful?’ And: ‘Hey, you’ve got all these brilliant people, but they all seem to be men.’”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "O’Mara adds: “She was going against gendered expectations but also, to become the female Steve Jobs, she made herself less feminine and also made herself less young.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Holmes ran the company with Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani, a businessman 19 years her senior, while keeping their romantic relationship a secret. Together they raised $945m. Theranos had published no peer-reviewed data but Holmes was a charismatic and persuasive presence in boardrooms.", "links": [{"text": "Theranos", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/technology/theranos"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Agus, a professor of medicine who is chief executive of the Ellison Medical Institute , comments: “You know how you go into a room and there could be 10 people at a table and everyone’s having a discussion? All of a sudden one person speaks and the entire room goes: ‘Yeah, I’ll go that direction.’ She had that ability.", "links": [{"text": "Ellison Medical Institute", "url": "https://ellisonmedicalinstitute.org/people/david-agus/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I saw how she was able to sway people. That characteristic is great if you’re a Steve Jobs. That characteristic is very difficult in health because we should be data-driven, not swayed by personalities.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "By 2014 Theranos was valued at $9bn. Holmes was named the youngest female self-made billionaire in the US with a net worth of $4.5bn by the time she was 30. She was celebrated on magazine covers and in power lists."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The New Yorker wrote : “Although she can quote Jane Austen by heart, she no longer devotes time to novels or friends, doesn’t date, doesn’t own a television, and hasn’t taken a vacation in ten years. Her refrigerator is all but empty, as she eats most of her meals at the office. She is a vegan, and several times a day she drinks a pulverized concoction of cucumber, parsley, kale, spinach, romaine lettuce, and celery.”", "links": [{"text": "The New Yorker wrote", "url": "https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2014/12/15/blood-simpler"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/d4891b1cd57d2fc96007cf8c0eed587df9506640/0_0_3500_2333/master/3500.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Elizabeth Holmes in 2015", "caption": "Elizabeth Holmes in 2015. Photograph: Brendan McDermid/Reuters", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The heady atmosphere seduced elder statesmen such as Shultz, who had served as a bridge between Washington and Silicon Valley during the Ronald Reagan era. Despite no specialist expertise in laboratory diagnostics, he joined the Theranos board in 2011, when he was in his 90s. O’Mara says: “He was drawn in by the idea that here is a bright young person trying to do something more meaningful than building an app. But there wasn’t enough due diligence.”", "links": [{"text": "Ronald Reagan", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/books/2024/oct/08/reagan-his-life-and-legend-by-max-boot-review-a-head-of-state-lost-without-a-script"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In his biography, In the Nation’s Service , journalist Philip Taubman describes how people around Shultz worried that his enthusiasm had become entangled with personal affection for Holmes. Shultz spoke to her by phone almost daily and invited her to family Christmas dinners. Holmes encouraged his attention, leaning in close when they sat together.", "links": [{"text": "In the Nation’s Service", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/books/2023/jan/10/george-shultz-biography-theranos-elizabeth-holmes"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Shultz even encouraged his grandson, Tyler Shultz , to take a summer internship at Theranos before joining the company full-time. Tyler eventually became convinced that Holmes was exaggerating what her technology could do. He took his concerns to the Wall Street Journal, whose investigation into the company was crucial to unravelling its web of deceit.", "links": [{"text": "Tyler Shultz", "url": "https://www.tyler-shultz.com/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Holmes suspected Tyler was behind the disclosures. Her lawyers pursued him and he was placed under surveillance, leaving him afraid and looking to his grandfather for protection. But George Shultz declined to break with Holmes. According to Taubman, he tried unsuccessfully to mediate between the two rather than stand by his grandson. George Shultz died in 2021 at the age of 100."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Scientists also had their doubts about Holmes’s grand promises. Agus recalls: “The problem with blood is it clots and, when you do these small fluidics, it clogs. She wouldn’t give me an answer of why that wasn’t a problem for her. To me, that was the initial red flag. The emperor with no clothes was evident in that she was either ultra-secretive, or the way she was trying to explain things didn’t make sense.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "John Ioannidis , a professor of medicine and health research at Stanford University, happened to work in a building that had previously served as Theranos’s headquarters. In 2015, he published a Journal of the American Medical Association (Jama) commentary highlighting the striking absence of peer-reviewed evidence supporting Theranos’s claims.", "links": [{"text": "John Ioannidis", "url": "https://med.stanford.edu/profiles/john-ioannidis"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "He says: “They wanted me to recant and meet with Elizabeth Holmes , and maybe write together some new Jama piece saying that I had seen the light.” When Ioannidis urged them to publish validation data, Theranos cited 100-plus patent filings. “I looked at these patents and they were mostly nonsensical. One had a title close to ‘How to do clinical research’ – vague and non-specific. None of that covered the gap of what was being done.”", "links": [{"text": "Elizabeth Holmes", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/elizabeth-holmes"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/5d622760c33b9fccd3f8f529efefe89dca334078/0_0_855_570/master/855.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Elizabeth Holmes walks past yellow caution tape near trees at a prison camp", "caption": "Elizabeth Holmes at federal prison camp Bryan in 2025. Photograph: Adrees Latif/Reuters", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But in assessing Holmes’s motivations, Ioannidis offers a nuanced view. “I don’t think anyone can be in her mind. My most likely interpretation is that she believed she would start that wave – attract capital, funds, talent, expertise – and make this real."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I don’t think she was purely a charlatan. She was power-driven, but in Silicon Valley so many people are power-driven. She saw that the way to do this was to get power first, and then attract the people and technology to materialise it.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Holmes quit as chief executive in 2018 and the company collapsed that year. The trial of Holmes resulted in her 2022 sentencing to more than 11 years in prison for fraud and conspiracy. The scandal was chronicled in a book, multiple podcasts and the biographical mini-series The Dropout that starred Amanda Seyfried.", "links": [{"text": "The Dropout", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2022/mar/03/the-dropout-review-another-mind-blowing-portrait-of-a-great-american-fraudster"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "You Can See Everything offers an intimate, often bewildering glimpse into Holmes’s domestic life with her partner, Billy Evans , and their two young children during the 34 days before she reported to prison in May 2023.", "links": [{"text": "Billy Evans", "url": "https://www.businessinsider.com/elizabeth-holmes-fiance-partner-billy-evans-relationship-job-theranos"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Lavalier’s microphones capture Holmes’s every breath as she reads bedtime stories to the children, sometimes for 12 hours a day. Evans, meanwhile, is filmed naked in the shower and whisking eggs as he corrects her cooking. They fixate on past media profiles, arguing that journalists fabricated her persona."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The biggest revelation occurs off-camera. article_text:
D avid Agus’s first encounter with Elizabeth Holmes at a health conference came as a shock. The Holmes he met in the green room was personable and pleasant. The Holmes he interviewed on stage was altogether different.

“The accent changed: this deep voice, very serious,” Agus, a medical oncologist , recalls by phone from Los Angeles. “It was as if I had met a person and then interviewed a separate person. That transition from the green room to the stage – I had never experienced something like that before.”

Holmes is not like you or me. She was still a teenager when she founded Theranos, touting technology capable of performing medical tests using only a few drops of blood. She cultivated a distinctive persona: blond hair, an unblinking gaze, a husky voice and a black turtleneck worn in homage to Apple co-founder Steve Jobs .

Holmes mesmerised investors and board members including Rupert Murdoch, Larry Ellison, Carlos Slim and former secretaries of state Henry Kissinger and George Shultz. She became America’s youngest self-made female billionaire. But it was all an illusion, a confidence trick built on a scam. Holmes’s shining career ended in disgrace and imprisonment.

Margaret O’Mara , a history professor at the University of Washington in Seattle and author of The Code: Silicon Valley and the Remaking of America, says: “You can’t make this stuff up. If some screenwriter had tried to manufacture this out of whole cloth people would be like, no, this is an unbelievable story. Yet it’s real. Who’s the real Elizabeth Holmes? That’s a question that still hasn’t been answered .”

Perhaps the answer lies in You Can See Everything , a reality-bending documentary, released in the US on Friday, in which Holmes goes eyeball-to-eyeball with the absurdist comedian Nathan Fielder, who directs along with Lance Oppenheim. It was filmed in the 34 days before she was due to report to federal prison camp Bryan in Texas to begin her 11-year sentence for wire fraud and conspiracy.

That fate seemed unthinkable in 2003 when, at the age of 19, Holmes dropped out of Stanford University and established Theranos , promising to revolutionise the multibillion-dollar blood-testing industry by using microfluidics to run hundreds of tests on just a few drops of blood.

She found a receptive audience among investors who wanted Silicon Valley to deliver more than Facebook friends. O’Mara explains: “ She stands out in her ascent as a female entrepreneur at a time when men were dominating the scene and she was doing something that was in tech but seemed to be change-the-world-tech.

“The techlash wasn’t brewing yet but, where there was criticism of Silicon Valley, it was like: ‘Hey, you’ve got all these brilliant people and all you’re doing is building apps? Why don’t you do something a little more meaningful?’ And: ‘Hey, you’ve got all these brilliant people, but they all seem to be men.’”

O’Mara adds: “She was going against gendered expectations but also, to become the female Steve Jobs, she made herself less feminine and also made herself less young.”

Holmes ran the company with Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani, a businessman 19 years her senior, while keeping their romantic relationship a secret. Together they raised $945m. Theranos had published no peer-reviewed data but Holmes was a charismatic and persuasive presence in boardrooms.

Agus, a professor of medicine who is chief executive of the Ellison Medical Institute , comments: “You know how you go into a room and there could be 10 people at a table and everyone’s having a discussion? All of a sudden one person speaks and the entire room goes: ‘Yeah, I’ll go that direction.’ She had that ability.

“I saw how she was able to sway people. That characteristic is great if you’re a Steve Jobs. That characteristic is very difficult in health because we should be data-driven, not swayed by personalities.”

By 2014 Theranos was valued at $9bn. Holmes was named the youngest female self-made billionaire in the US with a net worth of $4.5bn by the time she was 30. She was celebrated on magazine covers and in power lists.

The New Yorker wrote : “Although she can quote Jane Austen by heart, she no longer devotes time to novels or friends, doesn’t date, doesn’t own a television, and hasn’t taken a vacation in ten years. Her refrigerator is all but empty, as she eats most of her meals at the office. She is a vegan, and several times a day she drinks a pulverized concoction of cucumber, parsley, kale, spinach, romaine lettuce, and celery.”

The heady atmosphere seduced elder statesmen such as Shultz, who had served as a bridge between Washington and Silicon Valley during the Ronald Reagan era. Despite no specialist expertise in laboratory diagnostics, he joined the Theranos board in 2011, when he was in his 90s. O’Mara says: “He was drawn in by the idea that here is a bright young person trying to do something more meaningful than building an app. But there wasn’t enough due diligence.”

In his biography, In the Nation’s Service , journalist Philip Taubman describes how people around Shultz worried that his enthusiasm had become entangled with personal affection for Holmes. Shultz spoke to her by phone almost daily and invited her to family Christmas dinners. Holmes encouraged his attention, leaning in close when they sat together.

Shultz even encouraged his grandson, Tyler Shultz , to take a summer internship at Theranos before joining the company full-time. Tyler eventually became convinced that Holmes was exaggerating what her technology could do. He took his concerns to the Wall Street Journal, whose investigation into the company was crucial to unravelling its web of deceit.

Holmes suspected Tyler was behind the disclosures. Her lawyers pursued him and he was placed under surveillance, leaving him afraid and looking to his grandfather for protection. But George Shultz declined to break with Holmes. According to Taubman, he tried unsuccessfully to mediate between the two rather than stand by his grandson. George Shultz died in 2021 at the age of 100.

Scientists also had their doubts about Holmes’s grand promises. Agus recalls: “The problem with blood is it clots and, when you do these small fluidics, it clogs. She wouldn’t give me an answer of why that wasn’t a problem for her. To me, that was the initial red flag. The emperor with no clothes was evident in that she was either ultra-secretive, or the way she was trying to explain things didn’t make sense.”

John Ioannidis , a professor of medicine and health research at Stanford University, happened to work in a building that had previously served as Theranos’s headquarters. In 2015, he published a Journal of the American Medical Association (Jama) commentary highlighting the striking absence of peer-reviewed evidence supporting Theranos’s claims.

He says: “They wanted me to recant and meet with Elizabeth Holmes , and maybe write together some new Jama piece saying that I had seen the light.” When Ioannidis urged them to publish validation data, Theranos cited 100-plus patent filings. “I looked at these patents and they were mostly nonsensical. One had a title close to ‘How to do clinical research’ – vague and non-specific. None of that covered the gap of what was being done.”

But in assessing Holmes’s motivations, Ioannidis offers a nuanced view. “I don’t think anyone can be in her mind. My most likely interpretation is that she believed she would start that wave – attract capital, funds, talent, expertise – and make this real.

“I don’t think she was purely a charlatan. She was power-driven, but in Silicon Valley so many people are power-driven. She saw that the way to do this was to get power first, and then attract the people and technology to materialise it.”

Holmes quit as chief executive in 2018 and the company collapsed that year. The trial of Holmes resulted in her 2022 sentencing to more than 11 years in prison for fraud and conspiracy. The scandal was chronicled in a book, multiple podcasts and the biographical mini-series The Dropout that starred Amanda Seyfried.

You Can See Everything offers an intimate, often bewildering glimpse into Holmes’s domestic life with her partner, Billy Evans , and their two young children during the 34 days before she reported to prison in May 2023.

Lavalier’s microphones capture Holmes’s every breath as she reads bedtime stories to the children, sometimes for 12 hours a day. Evans, meanwhile, is filmed naked in the shower and whisking eggs as he corrects her cooking. They fixate on past media profiles, arguing that journalists fabricated her persona.

The biggest revelation occurs off-camera. Even as she prepared to enter prison, Holmes and Evans were actively planning a new medical tech startup. In 2025, two years into her sentence, Evans sought $18.5m for Haemanthus – a company allegedly holding patents for a device claiming to scan blood, urine and saliva samples using lasers.

Fool me once, shame on you; fool me twice, shame on me? As Silicon Valley pours unprecedented sums into artificial intelligence, O’Mara believes the lessons of Theranos extend well beyond Holmes herself. “ The cautionary tale is resonant to a broader Silicon Valley morality tale in putting so much faith and power in the hands of one young person or a small circle of people.

“The founder culture and obsession of Silicon Valley that helped Elizabeth Holmes become who she was is still alive and well and stronger than ever. We’ve never seen power and wealth more concentrated in so few hands. Not even in America’s Gilded Age have we seen this.”

You Can See Everything is out in the US now, in Australia on 12 November and in the UK on 20 November

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "纽约画廊主兼艺术家彼得·纳吉（Peter Nagy）逝世，享年67岁。他创立的Nature Morte画廊曾一度在柏林设有分支机构。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "据他联合创立的新德里Nature Morte画廊透露，他于10月13日经长期病治无效后逝世。纳吉是印度当代艺术界的重要代表人物之一，为推动该艺术界走向国际知名度做出了贡献。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Nagy于1959年出生于美国康涅狄格州布里奇波特，曾在纽约帕森斯设计学院学习传播设计、艺术史与艺术理论，并于1981年毕业。在1980年代初期，他最初以艺术家身份崭露头角。他的作品探讨了图像的传播与变迁、版权以及艺术的商业化。在此过程中，他运用了公司标志、广告图案以及艺术书籍中的图片等元素，将其制成拼贴画并进行复制。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "1982年，Nagy与艺术家Alan Belcher在纽约东村创立了Nature Morte画廊。这个展览空间成为了当时前卫艺术的重要阵地，早期便展出了Cady Noland、Louise Lawler、Sherrie Levine、Robert Gober和Gretchen Bender等艺术家的作品。1980年代中期，Nagy曾在纽约的International with Monument画廊等场所展出自己的艺术作品。1985年，作为艺术家集体Group Material的成员，他参与了惠特尼双年展；1987年，该集体在卡塞尔文献展上展出了作品。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "印度当代艺术的平台", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "1992年，纳吉移居印度。五年后，他在新德里重新开办了Nature Morte画廊，并将该画廊发展成为该地区当代艺术的重要平台。其展览项目包括苏博德·古普塔（Subodh Gupta）、巴尔蒂·克her（Bharti Kher）、吉蒂什·卡拉特（Jitish Kallat）以及Raqs媒体小组（Raqs Media Collective）。该画廊同时也代理国际艺术立场，后来将其业务扩展至孟买。通过各种展览和艺博会亮相，纳吉为将印度当代艺术推向国际观众做出了重大贡献。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "从2008年到2014年，纳吉在柏林运营着Nature Morte的一个分支机构，起初位于齐默大街（Zimmerstraße），后来迁至魏丁格大街（Weydingerstraße）。在柏林，他曾举办达亚尼塔·辛格（Dayanita Singh）、图克拉尔与塔格拉（Thukral & Tagra）以及安妮塔·杜布（Anita Dube）等人的个展。该画廊以迈克尔·布勒-罗斯（Michael Bühler-Rose）和A·A·布朗森（A. A. Bronson）的双人展结束了其柏林篇章。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "最近，纳吉自身的艺术创作也再度受到更多的关注。2020年，纽约画廊主杰弗里·戴奇（Jeffrey Deitch）携手洋红平原（Magenta Plains）画廊为他举办了一场展览，重新审视了他的早期作品及其对图像再生产、日益增长的企业权力和全球资本流动的探讨。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Nature Morte在一份声明中高度评价纳吉是一位无畏、不羁且自由生活的人。四十多年来，他凭着直觉、坚定和忠诚支持着艺术家们。遵照他的愿望，该画廊在他去世后将继续营业。声明称，展览不应属于画廊，而应属于艺术家和公众。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Der New Yorker Galerist und Künstler Peter Nagy, dessen Galerie Nature Morte zeitweise auch in Berlin eine Dependance betrieb, ist im Alter von 67 Jahren gestorben

Er starb am 13. Oktober nach längerer Krankheit, wie die von ihm mitgegründete Galerie Nature Morte in Neu-Delhi mitteilte. Nagy gehörte zu den prägenden Persönlichkeiten der zeitgenössischen Kunstszene Indiens und trug dazu bei, sie international bekannt zu machen.

Nagy wurde 1959 in Bridgeport im US-Bundesstaat Connecticut geboren und studierte Kommunikationsdesign, Kunstgeschichte und Kunsttheorie an der Parsons School of Design in New York, wo er 1981 seinen Abschluss machte. In den frühen 1980er-Jahren trat er zunächst als Künstler in Erscheinung. Seine Arbeiten beschäftigten sich mit der Verbreitung und Veränderung von Bildern, mit Urheberschaft und der Kommerzialisierung von Kunst. Dabei verwendete er unter anderem Firmenlogos, Werbemotive und Abbildungen aus Kunstbüchern, die er zu Collagen verarbeitete und anschließend vervielfältigte.

1982 gründete Nagy gemeinsam mit dem Künstler Alan Belcher die Galerie Nature Morte im New Yorker East Village. Der Ausstellungsraum wurde zu einem wichtigen Ort der damaligen Avantgarde und zeigte früh Arbeiten von Künstlerinnen und Künstlern wie Cady Noland, Louise Lawler, Sherrie Levine, Robert Gober und Gretchen Bender. Nagy stellte seine eigene Kunst Mitte der 1980er-Jahre unter anderem in der New Yorker Galerie International with Monument aus. 1985 war er als Mitglied des Künstlerkollektivs Group Material an der Whitney Biennale beteiligt; 1987 präsentierte das Kollektiv Arbeiten auf der Documenta in Kassel.

Plattform für zeitgenössische Kunst aus Indien

1992 zog Nagy nach Indien. Fünf Jahre später eröffnete er Nature Morte in Neu-Delhi neu und entwickelte die Galerie zu einer bedeutenden Plattform für zeitgenössische Kunst aus der Region. Zum Programm gehörten unter anderem Subodh Gupta, Bharti Kher, Jitish Kallat und das Raqs Media Collective. Die Galerie vertrat zugleich internationale Positionen und erweiterte ihre Präsenz später um einen Standort in Mumbai. Mit Ausstellungen und Messeauftritten trug Nagy wesentlich dazu bei, indische Gegenwartskunst einem internationalen Publikum näherzubringen.

Von 2008 bis 2014 betrieb Nagy eine Dependance von Nature Morte in Berlin, zunächst in der Zimmerstraße, dann in der Weydingerstraße. In Berlin zeigte er unter anderem Einzelausstellungen von Dayanita Singh, Thukral & Tagra und Anita Dube. Die Galerie schloss ihr Berliner Kapitel mit einer Doppelschau von Michael Bühler-Rose und A. A. Bronson.

Zuletzt war auch Nagys eigenes künstlerisches Werk wieder stärker in den Blick gerückt. 2020 widmete ihm der New Yorker Galerist Jeffrey Deitch gemeinsam mit Magenta Plains eine Ausstellung, die seine frühen Arbeiten und deren Auseinandersetzung mit Bildreproduktion, wachsender Unternehmensmacht und globalen Kapitalströmen neu beleuchtete.

In einer Mitteilung würdigte Nature Morte Nagy als Person, die furchtlos, unangepasst und frei gelebt habe. Mehr als vier Jahrzehnte lang habe er Künstlerinnen und Künstler mit Instinkt, Konsequenz und Loyalität unterstützt. Entsprechend seinem Wunsch bleibt die Galerie nach seinem Tod geöffnet. Ausstellungen sollten, so die Mitteilung, nicht der Galerie gehören, sondern den Künstlerinnen und Künstlern und dem Publikum.

article_text:
美しい紅葉、豊かな食、芸術文化など、秋の京都は様々な魅力を満喫できる特別な季節。11月上旬には、「Art Collaboration Kyoto 2026」「CURATION⇄FAIR Kyoto」といった大規模アートフェアが開催され、多くのアートファンを惹きつける。ここでは日本美術からデザイン、現代アートまで、この秋、京都で見たい20の展覧会をピックアップ。紅葉狩りと美術館巡り、京都ならではの贅沢な時間を過ごしてみてはいかがだろうか。

◎アートフェア

「Art Collaboration Kyoto 2026」（国立京都国際会館ほか）

「コラボレーション」をコンセプトにした国際的アートフェア。「ギャラリーコラボレーション」と「キョウトミーティング」のふたつのセクションを設け、出展ギャラリーが作品の展示・販売を行うほか、ACKが主催するACK Curatesの「パブリックプログラム」、パートナー企業とコラボレーションした「スペシャルプログラム」などを展開する。そのほか、キッズプログラムやトークなど、これからのアートの担い手を育成する教育プログラムも実施。あわせて会期中には、京都府内で多数のアート展示が開催される。ニュースは こちら 。

会場： 国立京都国際会館 ほか 会期：11月7日〜11月9日

「Art Collaboration Kyoto（ACK）」が新ディレクション体制へ。7名のディレクターによる「リーダーシップコミッティー」へ移行

4月1日より始動。現フェアディレクターの山下有佳子はACK AmbassadorsのChairpersonに

「CURATION⇄FAIR Kyoto」（大本山 妙顕寺ほか）

美術のアカデミックな領域とマーケットの循環を促進することを目指す「CURATION⇄FAIR」が3日間開催される。2回目となる今回は、会場を「大本山 妙顕寺」、「本山 本法寺」、「本山 妙覺寺」の三寺院へと拡大。茶の湯、祈り、芸術の精神が受け継がれる西陣を舞台に、古美術や工芸、近代美術から現代美術までの多様な作品を展示販売する。出展者は、メルボルンを拠点とするアーティストランスペース、開廊1周年を迎えたギャラリー、100年以上の歴史をもつ老舗、コンテンポラリージュエリーや北欧陶器を専門に扱うギャラリーなど、多様な専門性をもつ33軒。

会場： 大本山 妙顕寺 会期：11月6日〜11月8日

◎日本美術

「特別展 源氏物語 王朝のかがやき」（京都国立博物館）

紫式部 によって著された『源氏物語』を、美術と文化の広がりから紹介する大規模展。光源氏をめぐる恋愛模様や人生模様は、後世に読み継がれるなかで、絵画、工芸、写本、芸能など多彩な表現を生み出してきた。本展では、源氏物語にまつわる絵画や工芸品、写本、注釈類など約250点を紹介する。京都国立博物館での源氏物語展は、約50年ぶりの開催となる。

会場： 京都国立博物館 会期：10月6日〜11月29日

「愛のカタチ ー幻の春画《稚児草紙》公開ー」（福田美術館）

本展で初めて一般公開される《稚児草紙》は、14世紀初めに制作された稚児と僧侶らとの親密な関係を詞書とともに記した絵巻で、模写や書籍等を通じて実在することだけが知られていた、幻の春画。また、男女の営みを描いた日本最古の春画のひとつである《小柴垣草紙》を江戸時代の絵師・ 谷文晁 が写した巻物も併せて展示。さらに 月岡雪鼎 らが手がけた肉筆による春画、そして 葛飾北斎 の傑作《波千鳥》に加え、 上村松園 や 鏑木清方 らが描いた「愛」にまつわる作品も展示する。

会場： 福田美術館 会期：9月19日〜2027年1月17日 ミューぽん で100円OFF！

「絵で知る、もっと楽しむ京都」（嵯峨嵐山文華館）

《洛中洛外図屏風》（前期展示）や《洛外図屏風》（後期展示）、 原在中 （1750〜1837）の《葵祭之図》など、今日でも親しまれている京の名所や行事、伝統文化を描いた作品を展示する。さらに、芸舞妓や京野菜など、京都ならではの画題を扱った作品をはじめ、 富岡鉄斎 （1836〜1924）や 池田遙邨 （1895〜1988）らが意匠を凝らした、和菓子の包装紙も並ぶ。絵画やデザインを通して、京都の魅力や暮らし、文化をあらためて楽しむことができそうだ。

会場： 嵯峨嵐山文華館 会期：10月3日〜2027年2月28日

◎現代アート

ウーゴ・ロンディノーネ「静寂のかたち」（音羽山 清水寺）

スイス出身のアーティスト、 ウーゴ・ロンディノーネ にとって、日本初となる個展。自然を風景としてだけでなく、人間の身体や精神、広大な時間の流れと結びつけてとらえてきたロンディノーネが、清水寺に17体の石の人物彫刻と太陽を描いた絵画、僧侶をかたどった彫刻を設置する。イヌクシュクを思わせる原初的な造形は、寺院の建築や庭園と呼応し、現代美術と古くから続く精神的な風景をつなぐ。人間の営みと自然、永続と無常の関係に思いをめぐらせる機会となる。

会場： 音羽山 清水寺 会期：10月27日〜11月12日

「Lightseeing Kyoto South 2026」（hatoba Galleryほか）

京都駅東部・東南部エリアを舞台に、京都で活動する若手アーティストによる作品展示やトークイベント、ワークショップなどを開催する周遊型アートイベント。2年目となる本年は、会場を4ヶ所に拡大し、10組以上のアーティストやグループ、プロジェクトが参加する。「Lightseeing」という言葉は、「sightseeing＝観光／名所を見ること」を踏まえながら、その焦点を「見るべき対象」から「見え方そのもの」へと移すための造語。地域の人々とアーティストの対話や協働を取り入れ、人と人、人と環境のあいだに新たな関係性を育み、アートが街の風景に自然と溶け込むことを目指す。ニュースは こちら 。

会場： hatoba Gallery 会期：10月24日〜11月23日

観光地から少し外れた京都へ。市営住宅や駅ビルをめぐる「Lightseeing Kyoto South 2026」が開幕

京都市立芸術大学の移転をきっかけに始まったアートイベント「Lightseeing Kyoto South 2026」。団地の各室で音や衣服、映像の作品が展開し、大学や高校の作品展示も並ぶ。会期は11月23日まで、金土日祝のみ開催

田中功起「時間がない（ときに眠ること）」（京都芸術センター）

京都芸術センターが、実績を積み重ねてきた中堅アーティストを個展形式で取り上げるシリーズ企画「FOCUS」の第7回として開催される本展。 田中功起 は、映像や執筆などによって「共に生きるとは何か」をテーマに、人々の協働や共同体の在り方を問い直す芸術実践を行ってきた。近年は、育児とケアの視点からアートをとらえ直す制作、執筆活動を続けている。

会場： 京都芸術センター 会期：11月6日〜2027年1月11日

「現代美術家 土佐尚子展『生成されるものたち』 ―アート＆テクノロジーの現在地―」（京都市京セラ美術館）

映像や音、身体、自然現象、人工生命などを横断しながら、約40年にわたり表現を追求してきた 土佐尚子 の大規模個展。ニューヨーク近代美術館（MoMA）収蔵の初期作品《An Expression》をはじめ、《Sound of Ikebana》《Genesis》《うつろひ》などの代表作から、初公開となる新作《土佐琳派：気韻生動》までを紹介する。日本文化に内在する美意識を起点に、音や映像、身体と自然現象の関係を通して探求してきた「かたちが生まれる仕組み」に迫る。

会場： 京都市京セラ美術館 会期：11月7日〜11月22日

吉田真一郎「意識の白」（HOSOO GALLERY）

美術家であり、麻布の蒐集家・研究家としても知られる 吉田真一郎 による展覧会。約40年にわたり蒐集・研究してきた大麻と苧麻の白布を用いた新作《白》を公開する。素材や織りのわずかな違いから浮かび上がる「白」の多様な表情に加え、千点を超える蒐集資料を再構成した新作インスタレーションも展示。布の物質性を超えて、「見ること」や「意識」のあり方を問い直す。

会場： HOSOO GALLERY 会期：11月6日〜2027年3月20日

森万里子「Shrine II ─ 内なる光のトポロジー」（タイム堂ギャラリー）

一般財団法人未来文化創造財団は、文化が持続的に発展する社会基盤づくりの活動のひとつとして、京都御所の西南にタイム堂ギャラリーをオープン。こけら落としとして、人類と宇宙との関係を考察する作品で知られる 森万里子 の個展を開催する。空間の中核をなす立体インスタレーションと、壁面を囲む平面作品で構成される本展は、作品群の共鳴によって、ギャラリー全体をひとつの「知覚の装置（アパラタス）」へと変容させる。ニュースは こちら 。

会場： タイム堂ギャラリー 会期：11月6日〜2027年3月31日

タイム堂ギャラリーが京都御所の西南に11月オープン。こけら落としは「森 万里子：Shrine II ─ 内なる光のトポロジー」

会期は11月6日〜2027年3月31日

◎建築、デザイン、写真

「時がかたちづくる建築 －TIME’Sと安藤忠雄－」（京都建築センター）

京都建築センターが入居するTIME'Sは、1984年に建築家・ 安藤忠雄 の設計で誕生した。本展では、「時間」という名を与えられたTIME'Sという建築を通して、人の手でつくられる建造物でありながら、同時に時間とともにかたちづくられていく存在としての建築について考える。知られざる建設前の景色や、建設中の写真、また竣工後の世間の受け止め方や使われ方を当時の雑誌などから浮かび上がらせ 、またオリジナルのドローイングや模型を読み取りながら、安藤がタイムズの設計にあたって考えた思考の軌跡をたどる。

会場： 京都建築センター 会期：9月2日〜11月23日

「カイ・フランク展 時代を超えるフィンランド・デザイン」（美術館「えき」KYOTO）

フィンランドの伝説的デザイナー、 カイ・フランク （1911〜89）。フィンランドのヴィープリ、現在のロシアに生まれ、ヘルシンキの中央工芸学校、現在のアアルト大学の家具デザイン科を卒業したのち、インテリアやテキスタイルのデザインに携わった。本展は、ヘルシンキ建築＆デザイン・ミュージアムのコレクションを中心に、ガラスや陶磁器、ファブリック、デザイン画など250点以上で、カイ・フランクの仕事を包括的に紹介する。

会場： 美術館「えき」KYOTO 会期：11月3日〜12月20日

「Superplay －ロッテルダムのグラフィックデザイン」（京都dddギャラリー）

オランダ・ロッテルダムを拠点とするグラフィックデザインスタジオ、Studio SpassとTeam Thursdayによる展覧会。タイポグラフィを軸に、遊び心あふれるヴィジュアルアイデンティティや出版物、空間オブジェクトを手がける両スタジオの作品を紹介する。紙の枠を超えて空間へと広がるグラフィックデザインに着目し、アムステルダムを中心に知られるダッチデザインとは異なる、港町ロッテルダムならではのデザインの魅力を探る。

会場： 京都dddギャラリー 会期：11月4日〜2027年1月13日

マルティーヌ・フランク「時代への視線」（何必館・京都現代美術館）

「時代への眼差し」をテーマに、パリを拠点に活躍したマグナム・フォトの写真家、 マルティーヌ・フランク の作品を紹介する。子供やポートレイト、アイルランド、夫アンリ・カルティエ＝ブレッソンとその仲間たちをテーマに、何必館コレクションから厳選したサイン入りオリジナルプリント60点を展示。家族だからこそとらえられたブレッソンの素顔などを通して、社会や人々に向けられたフランクの豊かなまなざしに迫る。

染織芸術のパイオニア、 山鹿清華 の40年ぶりとなる回顧展。デザイン、素材の選択、制作までを作家自身が一貫して手がける「手織錦」を生み出し、染織を美術表現として切り拓いた作家の歩みを紹介する。祇園祭のタペストリーや、建築家・ 村野藤吾 との協働による空間装飾など、代表作と資料を通してその知られざる創作の軌跡をたどる。レポートは こちら 。

「没後100年記念 住友春翠 －仕合せの住友近代美術コレクション」（泉屋博古館）

住友家第15代当主・ 住友春翠 の没後100年を記念し、春翠が関心を寄せた近代美術に焦点を当てる。明治中頃から大正時代にかけて、同時代の作家たちとの交流を通じて作品を収集した春翠。本展では、作品との出会いを時系列に沿ってたどりながら、その美意識をひもとく。「家」と「私」というふたつの意識を手がかりに、収集の背景や時代性から住友コレクションの形成史を見つめ直す。

title_original: NOUVELLE STAR · Léa Favre : « Faire jouer une agression, ça me mettrait mal à l’aise. Avec des marionnettes, c’est différent. »
editorial_title_zh: 新星 · 莉娅·法夫尔：“让真人去演一场袭击，我会觉得很不舒服。但如果是木偶，情况就不同了。”
editorial_excerpt_zh: 她令人震撼的动画短片处女作《Qui part à la chasse》在9月初的西卢埃特电影节（festival Silhouette）上荣获了由《TROISCOULEURS》编辑部颁发的最佳学校影片奖。本文将为您走近这位内敛剧情片创作者的肖像，她梦想着让自己的电影替她发声。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "image", "url": "https://www.troiscouleurs.fr/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Lea-Favre-c-Valentin-De-Steur--819x1024.png", "alt": "Lea Favre c Valentin De Steur", "caption": "", "credit": "Trois Couleurs", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "凭借清脆的嗓音和模范小学生般的发型，你很难看出莉娅·法夫尔已经29岁了。她回忆说，自己小时候并没有和家人一起去电影院的记忆，甚至在看过电影之前就产生了拍电影的念头。透过视频连线，这位从出生地瑞士接受我们采访的年轻导演在讲述自己担任克劳德·巴拉斯（Claude Barras）动画长片《野性》（2024年）实习制片助理的经历时，棕色的眼睛里闪烁着光芒。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "曾执导《西葫芦的生活》（2016年）的导演团队部分成员随后协助这位年轻电影人制作了《Qui part à la chasse》。这部作品呼应了她个人的经历，性格内敛的她通过短片讲述了自己某天突然被一个偶然遇得的男子困住的遭遇。她曾在洛桑大学学习真人实景电影，后就读于洛桑艺术学院（ECAL），她谈到了自己为何大胆选择定格动画：“在这个框架下，这让我能够重新掌控局势。让真人去演一场袭击，我会觉得很不舒服。但如果是木偶，情况就不同了。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "影片核心处，画面消失了，唯有那个男人的话语在回响。这实际上是导演现场抓录的陌生人真实录音。其目的何在？是通过音轨将观众和女主角置于同一处境：“这必须是场噩梦。”莉娅·法夫尔刚刚入选“银幕战争”电影节（War on Screen）编剧驻留计划。这位值得密切关注和倾听的艺术家，正蓄力为下一部动画电影赋予生命。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "关注我们", "translated": true}]

Elle qui, petite, n’a pas le souvenir d’être allée au cinéma en famille, dit avoir eu envie de faire des films avant d’en voir. Force est de constater que ses yeux bruns pétillent lorsqu’elle nous raconte, en visio depuis sa Suisse natale, son expérience en tant qu’assistante de production stagiaire sur le tournage de Sauvages (2024) de Claude Barras."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Une partie de l’équipe du réalisateur de Ma vie de courgette (2016) a ensuite accompagné la jeune cinéaste dans la fabrication de Qui part à la chasse. Celle qui a appris à faire du cinéma en prise de vue réelle à l’université de Lausanne, puis à l’École cantonale d’art de Lausanne (ECAL) explique son choix audacieux du stop motion : « Dans ce cadre-là, cela me permet de reprendre le contrôle sur la situation. Faire jouer une agression, ça me mettrait mal à l’aise. Avec des marionnettes, c’est différent. »"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Au cœur du film, l’image disparaît, ce qui laisse résonner les paroles de l’homme. Il s’agit en fait d’un enregistrement réel de l’inconnu, pris sur le vif par la réalisatrice. Le but ? article_text:
Avec sa voix claire et sa coiffure d’écolière modèle, on donnerait difficilement à Lea Favre ses 29 ans. Elle qui, petite, n’a pas le souvenir d’être allée au cinéma en famille, dit avoir eu envie de faire des films avant d’en voir. Force est de constater que ses yeux bruns pétillent lorsqu’elle nous raconte, en visio depuis sa Suisse natale, son expérience en tant qu’assistante de production stagiaire sur le tournage de Sauvages (2024) de Claude Barras.

Une partie de l’équipe du réalisateur de Ma vie de courgette (2016) a ensuite accompagné la jeune cinéaste dans la fabrication de Qui part à la chasse. Écrit en écho à son histoire personnelle, la jeune femme au tempérament réservé y raconte le jour où elle s’est brusquement retrouvée prise au piège par un homme rencontré par hasard. Celle qui a appris à faire du cinéma en prise de vue réelle à l’université de Lausanne, puis à l’École cantonale d’art de Lausanne (ECAL) explique son choix audacieux du stop motion : « Dans ce cadre-là, cela me permet de reprendre le contrôle sur la situation. Faire jouer une agression, ça me mettrait mal à l’aise. Avec des marionnettes, c’est différent. »

Au cœur du film, l’image disparaît, ce qui laisse résonner les paroles de l’homme. Il s’agit en fait d’un enregistrement réel de l’inconnu, pris sur le vif par la réalisatrice. Le but ? Mettre le spectateur et l’héroïne au même niveau par l’intermédiaire de la bande-son : « Il fallait que ce soit cauchemardesque. » Lea Favre vient d’être sélectionnée pour participer à la résidence d’écriture du festival War on Screen. De quoi donner vie au prochain film d’animation d’une artiste à suivre et à écouter attentivement.

article_text:
A favorite on the festival circuit since its premiere last year, Dennis Cooper and Zac Farley’s Room Temperature is finally getting a release this month from Altered Innocence. Ahead of a VOD, Blu-ray, and DVD debut on November 24th of the off-center family-drama-turned-ghost-story ( and a John Waters favorite ), we’re pleased to exclusively debut the trailer.

Here’s the synopsis: “Every Halloween, a family living in the barren sprawl of the California desert transforms their home into a DIY haunted house attraction for the neighborhood. What used to be a group effort has increasingly become the dad’s obsessive fantasy that his family is expected to enact. Hilarious, uncomfortable, and deeply strange, ROOM TEMPERATURE is haunted-house cinema as poetic autopsy, a slow, disquieting meditation on control, longing, and the fantasies we force onto others. Novelist Dennis Cooper (The George Miles Cycle and The Sluts) & visual artist Zac Farley (PERMANENT GREEN LIGHT) team up once more to create a movie that John Waters called ‘weird, creepy, and maybe… just maybe, great’.”

“The whole idea was not to make things scary––it was to present the mechanics of what would be scary,” Cooper told us ahead of the New York premiere last fall . “No one seems even remotely scared in the film. They’re all kind of bemused at most. The film has this false start: at the beginning you see the house, and it’s playing this crazy music, and the lights are going on and off, and it looks like it’s going to be really scary. But then by the time he actually gets inside the house, it just turns out to be a really shitty haunted house.”

See the exclusive trailer below, and pre-order the Blu-ray, DVD, and digital release here .

title_original: Interview: Jim Jarmusch on Father Mother Sister Brother
editorial_title_zh: 访谈：吉姆·贾木许谈《Father Mother Sister Brother》
editorial_excerpt_zh: 家庭关系：这位传奇的美国电影人谈论了他的最新力作，一幅关于父母与子女的妙趣横生、哀伤而又挥之不去的肖像画
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "人们不得不回溯到1984年的《天堂陌客》，才能在吉姆·贾木许（Jim Jarmusch）的作品中找到一部像《Father Mother Sister Brother》这样妙趣横生、哀伤而又令人难忘的分段式电影。该片赢得了今年威尼斯电影节的金狮奖——对于这样一部内敛的家庭题材电影而言，这是一个非同寻常的成就。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《Father Mother Sister Brother》拥有莫扎特室内乐般的细腻与错综复杂。三个故事分别发生在三个不同的国家，每个故事都有着各自的父母与子女组合，它们在更广阔的意义上被血亲关系那种大都难以言喻的复杂性串联起来。电影开篇于新泽西州的一个乡村，亚当·德赖弗（Adam Driver）和玛丽亚姆·拜利克（Mayim Bialik）饰演的一对兄妹正在探望他们孤僻的父亲——一个由汤姆·维茨（Tom Waits）带着难以掩饰的恶作剧般快意所饰演的骗子。在第二段中，常住都柏林的畅销书作家夏洛特·兰普林（Charlotte Rampling）正为她的女儿们——凯特·布兰切特（Cate Blanchett）和薇姬·克里普斯（Vicky Krieps）——精心准备一份非常甜腻的下午茶，她们一年才获准探望她一次。直到以巴黎为背景的最后一段中，压抑至今的情感才终于爆发：一对二十多岁的双胞胎——由卢卡·萨巴特（Luka Sabbat）和因迪娅·摩尔（Indya Moore）饰演——在他们曾与在一场神秘空难中丧生的父母共同居住的公寓里收拾着童年纪念品和照片。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "凭借着让心灵和眼光都感到愉悦的三部曲之间既具隐喻性又具形式上的联系，《Father Mother Sister Brother》某种程度上是一部解谜电影，拼凑这些碎片揭示了一种对更深层结局的渴望，而这种结局对角色来说可能遥不可及，对我们而言至少也是一个开放式的问题。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我一直觉得你拍的电影大致分两种：一种是有角色、有人际关系和剧情的电影，另一种则是只有角色和人际关系的多元结构电影。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我明白你为什么会这么想。但对我来说，文学形式就是剧情。分段式体裁贯穿于文学之中，从《十日谈》到《坎特伯雷故事集》都是如此。[这种分段形式]在电影中也被大量使用。对我来说，它是一种讲述故事的结构。我用三周时间写完了《Father Mother Sister Brother》的剧本，但就像我的所有剧本一样，在此之前我一直在收集各种偶然涌现、毫无结构可言的琐碎素材。我这样做持续了八九个月。有些电影，这个收集过程长达数年。而且我总是从角色入手，为特定的演员进行创作。我只写一个剧本并用它来筹集资金。但我并不喜欢剧本，所以我不会费心去一遍又一遍地修改初稿。我们拍摄的是剧本的第二稿，而剪辑依据的则是下一稿。终剪版其实就是最终定稿。对于《Father Mother》来说，初稿仅仅是为我选定的演员编写台词。这是一个相当极简的东西——只是一种亲密、安静的互动。这部电影其实没有戏剧性。它没有动作戏，没有暴力，没有性，什么都没有。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你永远无法将这部电影中的各个故事剥离开来，因为它们是累积的。对我和巴黎的那段“Sister Brother”而言，它带有一点情感色彩，但如果你单独来看它就不会有这种感觉。《Father Mother Sister Brother》非常极简且充满观察性，但如果把这些部分作为短片单独放映，将会破坏[整体]作品。我在所有三个部分中都将插花用作一种隐喻。它非常细腻，拍摄时需要高度的专注，信不信由你。拍僵尸从地下钻出来追赶人们，可比留意某人的眼皮、手指的手势、说话的语气以及他们何时移开视线要容易得多——所有这些都非常非常小心翼翼。它非常聚焦。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "各部分之间有许多重复的元素：花朵、某种栗红色的东西，以及在每个部分快结束时，某个角色向窗外或门外张望。而在最后一部分中，兄妹俩走进了光芒之中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "而且每一段里都有开车兜风的镜头。还有滑板爱好者。并且提到了用各种饮品——茶、水——进行干杯。我的最后几部电影里都有关于水的元素。也有一些某种程度上会再次出现的小笑话。我当时试图在情感上构建另一种累积。我的电影不应该表达任何东西，也没有什么信息。我并不是在刻意拍一部煽情的电影，但是，你知道的，它涉及人与人之间微妙的关系，因此交换和观察情感的想法构成了整部电影的核心。对我而言是这样。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在这部作品之前，你的任何电影里探讨过父母与子女的关系吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在我的第一部电影《长假漫漫》（1980）中，[主角]去探望了他被关在收容所的母亲。让我想想——《天堂陌客》里，他们是表亲？《神秘列车》（1989），没有……我想其实真没有。我大概在17岁时离家出走，家庭这件事在我的作品中从来都不是一个重头戏——反正父母这部分不是。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但你是一位父亲。作为一个如今已步入青年期的孩子的父亲，这种经历是否融入了你的创作之中？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "没有任何有意识的融入。再说一次，我尽量不去刻意去寻找与我自身的联系。显然，它们确实存在于其中，但那是留给别人去分析或不予置评的事。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "父母与子女的关系是每个片段的核心。而且你会发现，孩子们之所以会成为现在这样，与他们的父母息息相关，哪怕每个片段中的两个兄弟姐妹彼此截然不同。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对，因为那是成为家庭一部分的体验。你能非常清晰地看到父母对孩子产生的影响，但这并不是评判性的。这是观察性的。我们现在生活在这个该死的世界里，同理心居然被认为是一种弱点，对吧？所以对我来说，我希望我做的每件事里都有一点同理心。这部电影当然也没有评判父母。夏洛特·兰普林的母亲设定了所有这些深思熟虑的界限，其中一个是她的治疗师建议的：她一年只和女儿们见一次面。你绝对能看到其中的影响。而第三个故事讲的是缺席与失落。父母已经不在了。这里面有一种悲伤，当你的父母不再陪伴在你的生活中时，这是你无法改变的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在电影中，那些亲密或家庭关系几乎从未显得可信。但在这里，这些关系通过角色的那些细微举动、他们对视的方式，以及每个人似乎都知道对方将会有什么反应的感觉，而显得真实。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "比如，当第一部分的父亲记不起他的儿子已经离婚时，姐姐抓住了这一点，她给了他一个暗示，他立刻就接上了。就是这些极小的细节。它们的节奏非常微妙，但对我来说整部电影给人的感觉就是这样。我常常精疲力竭地回到酒店之类的住处，因为注意力全放在人们的睫毛上。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你们拍了多少周？每个部分的拍摄时间各不相同吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们每个部分大约有10天拍摄时间，还有一些前期准备时间。我有不可思议的合作者：弗雷德·埃尔姆斯（摄影师）和马克·弗里德伯格（美术指导）负责在新泽西的第一部分，约里克·勒·索尔负责在爱尔兰的第二部分和在帕尔（译注：应指巴黎）的第三部分。我喜欢和约里克合作。他将拍摄我的下一部电影，那部片子全在巴黎拍摄。马尔科·比特纳·罗瑟担任法、爱两部分的美术指导。他做过《唯爱永生》（2013）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你说你是为特定的演员写作，但你如何与他们排练？你首先会和他们谈论各自的角色吗？因为这部电影里的某些人在进行非常具体的角色塑造。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "比如马伊姆·拜力克——我写这个剧本就是为了让她和亚当演姐弟。我以前不认识马伊姆，而且我也不知道她因之成名的那些电视剧。但我是一个《危险边缘！》迷，她是节目里我最喜欢的支持人，所以就是在看《危险边缘！》时，我脑海中浮现了她作为亚当·德赖弗姐姐的形象。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我其实不排练。我从不排练会出现在电影里的场景，因为表演在于回应，我不想提前把戏演出来。有时我会当场编排一些场景，让演员保持角色状态，或者我会分别跟他们聊聊各自的角色。我不喜欢用好像这个场景对每个人意义都一样的方式去跟他们交流。他们全都不一样。他们有不同的长处。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在我们和汤姆、亚当以及马伊姆拍摄的第一天结束后，汤姆把我拉到一边说：“听着，吉姆，你雇了这两个职业杀手。我该怎么办？”我告诉他按他自己的方式来。我知道他们更倾向于紧贴剧本，但汤姆需要更宽松的空间。我只是去发掘每个演员的长处。薇姬·克里普斯的处理方式与凯特·布兰切特大不相同。但我爱演员，我喜欢和他们一起玩。他们在好的意义上就像小孩子，因为他们奉命假扮成各种人，而他们自己的情感与经历就是他们的工具。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你以前和大多数演员都合作过，但没有和夏洛特·兰普林合作过，她太棒了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "哦天哪。真是一个了不起的人——聪明、美丽，而且是个伟大的演员。我简直疯狂地迷恋她。现在她管我叫她“不太秘密的崇拜者”，因为我无论何时在巴黎都喜欢见她。我以前也从未和薇姬·克里普斯合作过——她那么调皮又有趣——也没有和马伊姆·拜力克合作过，但其他人，是的。卢卡·萨巴特是个了不起的小伙子。他当时在洛杉矶，有大把的角色找上门来，然后他说：“你知道吗，我不想当黑人约翰尼·德普。我想在东京当DJ。我想去巴黎搞时尚。”他按照自己选择的方式生活。但他是个不错的演员。而因迪娅·摩尔是一位演员兼社会活动家。我曾在我为圣罗兰拍的那部小短片（2021年的《法国之水》）里和她合作过。她是个非凡的人。我很喜欢和她合作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些片段中有一个共同点，就是孩子们开车前往主要地点，在前两个部分中，他们也开车离开。你的电影里有很多开车的内容。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这在我们的生活中似乎是一件很普通的事。我喜欢那些不具戏剧性的时刻。当你从A点旅行到B点时，那通常脱离了戏剧性的故事。而当人们坐在车里时，他们都目视前方，所以他们不会像坐在桌子对面那样注意到每一个微小的面部表情或手势。他们的注意力非常不同。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "许多导演都说，让人们围坐在一张桌子旁是最难做到的事情。第二部分就出现了这种情况。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "嗯，是的，你无处可去。我得告诉你，所有这些场景都是在真实地点拍摄的。我们没有在搭景的摄影棚里。“父亲”所在的房子只有一个非常小的房间。我唯一拥有的、而且是随拍摄地点自带的东西，是一把可以旋转并望向那片湖泊的椅子，这非常重要，因为它就像是叫个暂停。我不知道你的过去如何，但当一个人和自己的家人在一起时，总得时不时地去他妈的歇一会儿，对吧？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "所以第二部分里的暂停就是对桌子的俯拍镜头吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我用高角度镜头也是为了省略时间，因为我不能直接切到另一个场景。当我深爱的剪辑师阿丰索·贡萨尔维斯（Affonso Gonçalves）梳理我们拍的所有素材时，他首先像拍电视剧那样把所有对话剪到了一起。结果整个片段只有四分钟长。但角色们本来应该在一起呆上两个小时，所以我们需要间歇和停顿。我想改变它的音乐节奏。停顿和对话一样重要，甚至对我来说更重要。那也是个非常小的房间，所以我设计成给每个人拍单人镜头，然后再拍三个不同的双人镜头。镜头覆盖范围很小，但都经过了极其仔细的规划。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们能聊聊片中的欺骗吗？父母对孩子并不是真的坦诚，反之亦然。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "是的，但我并不认为这是恶意的欺骗。汤姆· Waits 饰演的角色并不是个讨厌的人，但他大概是个糟糕的父亲。我没有去评判他们。他们都在扮演那些能满足某种情感需求的脚色。这让我想起我们如今生活的这个世界，里面有些人是邪恶的骗子，因为他们撒谎是为了逃避共情并操纵他人。但这些人，他们并不邪恶。如果他们有所欺骗——家庭就是这么复杂。", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "One would have to go back to 1984’s Stranger than Paradise to find in Jim Jarmusch’s work an episodic film as funny, sad, and haunting as Father Mother Sister Brother , which won the Golden Lion at this year’s Venice Film Festival—an unusual achievement for such an understated family picture."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Father Mother Sister Brother has the delicacy and intricacy of a Mozart chamber work. Three stories, each located in a separate country, each with its own arrangement of parents and children, are connected in a large sense by the mostly ineffable complexity of filial relationships. The film opens in rural New Jersey, where a brother and sister played by Adam Driver and Mayim Bialik are visiting their loner dad—a trickster, played with barely hidden glee by Tom Waits. In the second episode, Charlotte Rampling, a Dublin-based author of popular novels prepares a very sugary high tea for her daughters—Cate Blanchett and Vicky Krieps, who are only allowed to visit her once a year. It is only in the final episode, set in Paris, that the emotions which have been dammed up to this point, break out when a pair of twentysomething twins—played by Luka Sabbat and Indya Moore—pack up childhood mementos and photographs in the apartment where they lived with their parents, who died in a mysterious plane crash."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "With both metaphoric and formal connections between the three movements that delight the mind and the eye, Father Mother Sister Brother is a kind of puzzle film, where fitting the pieces together reveals a longing for a deeper resolution that may be out of reach for the characters, and is at least an open question for us."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I always think of you as making two different kinds of films: the films that have characters, relationships, and plot, and the multipart films that have just characters and relationships."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I see why you would think that. But for me, literary forms are plots. Episodic things run through literature, from The Decameron to The Canterbury Tales . [The episodic form] is used a lot in films. For me, it’s a structure that tells stories. I wrote the script for Father Mother Sister Brother in three weeks, but like with all my scripts, I had been gathering random things that just come to me with no structure. I did that for eight or nine months. With some films, it was years of gathering. And I always start with characters and write for specific actors. I write just one script and use it to get financing. But I don’t like scripts, so I don’t labor over draft after draft. The second draft of the script is what we shoot, and the next draft is what we edit. The final cut is just the final draft. With Father Mother , the first draft was just about writing dialogue for the actors I’d chosen. It’s quite a minimal thing—just sort of intimate, quiet interactions. The film has no drama, really. It has no action, it has no violence, it has no sex, it’s got nothing."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "You could never separate the stories in this film, because they accumulate. And for me, the Paris one, “Sister Brother,” is a bit emotional, but it would not be if you just looked at it alone. Father Mother Sister Brother is very minimal and very observational, but it would destroy the [overall] work to show the parts separately as short films. I used flower arrangements as a metaphor in all three sections. It’s very delicate, and it required a lot of focus in shooting it, believe it or not. It’s a lot easier to shoot zombies coming out of the ground and running after people than to be aware of someone’s eyelids and the gestures of their finger and the tone of their voice and when they look away—all of that was very, very careful. It was very focused."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "There are many repetitions from section to section: the flowers, something maroon, and toward the end of each section, a character looks out of a window or a door. And in the last section, the brother and sister walk into the light."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And there are car drives in each. And skateboarders. And references to toasting with various drinks—tea, water. There are water references in my last few films. There are little jokes that kind of recur as well. I was trying to build another kind of accumulation emotionally. My films are not supposed to say anything, and there’s no message. I’m not trying to make an emotional film, but, you know, it involves delicate relationships between people, and so the idea of feelings exchanged and observed is the heart of the whole film. For me."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Have you ever had parent-and-children relationships in any of your films before this?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In my first film, Permanent Vacation (1980), [the protagonist] goes to visit his mother, who’s institutionalized. Let’s see— Stranger Than Paradise , they’re cousins? Mystery Train (1989), no… I guess not, really. I kind of ran away from home when I was 17, and the family thing hasn’t really been a huge presence in my work—not the parental part, anyway."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But you are a parent. Did being a parent to a child who is now a young adult come into your writing of this?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Not in any conscious way. And again, I try not to be conscious of connections to myself. Obviously, they’re in there, but they’re for someone else to analyze or not."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The parent-child relationships are the center of each episode. And you see that the reason the children are the way they are has to do with the parent, even when the two siblings in each episode are very different from each other."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yeah, because that’s part of being in a family. You see that the parents affected their children very clearly, but it’s not judgmental. It’s observational. We live in this fucking world now where empathy is supposed to be a weakness, right? So for me, I hope there’s something empathetic in everything I do. And this one is certainly not judging the parents. Charlotte Rampling’s mother has all these deliberate boundaries, one of them suggested by her therapist: that she just see her daughters once a year. And you definitely see the effects. And the third story is about absence and loss. The parents are gone. There’s a kind of grief in that, and that’s something you can’t change when your parents are not there anymore in your life."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Those intimate or familial relationships are almost never believable in movies. But here the relationships feel real in the little things the characters do, the way they look at each other, and the way each seems to know how the other person is going to react."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For example, when the father in the first part fails to remember that his son is divorced, the sister catches him, she cues him, and he picks it up right away. Those are the tiny things. The timing of them is very delicate, but the whole film felt like that for me. I would go back to the hotel or whatever pretty exhausted from focusing on people’s eyelashes."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "How many weeks did you shoot? And did the shooting time vary for each section?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "We had about 10 days to shoot each section, and some prep time. I had incredible collaborators: Fred Elmes [cinematographer] and Mark Friedberg [production designer] for the first section in New Jersey, and Yorick Le Saux to shoot the second part in Ireland and the third part in Paris. I love working with Yorick. He’s going to shoot my next film, which is all in Paris. And Marco Bittner Rosser production-designed the French and Irish sections. He did Only Lovers Left Alive (2013)."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "You say you write for specific actors, but how do you rehearse with them? Do you talk to them about their characters first? Because some people in this film are doing really specific character work."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For example, Mayim Bialik—I wrote it for her and Adam to be brother and sister. I didn’t know Mayim, and I do not know the TV shows she’s famous for. But I’m a Jeopardy! fan, and she was my favorite host on the show, so it was while watching her on Jeopardy! that I imagined her as Adam Driver’s sister."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I don’t really rehearse. I never rehearse a scene that will be in the film, because acting is about reacting, and I don’t want to act it out in advance. Sometimes I make up scenes on the spot and have the actors be in character, or I talk with them separately about their characters. I don’t like talking to them as though the scene means the same for everyone. They’re all different. They have different strengths."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "After our first day of shooting with Tom, Adam, and Mayim, Tom took me aside and said, “So, Jim, you hired these two professional killers. What am I supposed to do?” And I told him just to do it his way. I know that they prefer to be tighter on the script, but Tom needs a longer leash. I just find the strengths of each actor. Vicky Krieps has a much different procedure than Cate Blanchett. But I love actors, and I love playing with them. They’re like children in a good way, in that they are pretending to be people on command, and their own emotions and experiences are their tools."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "You have worked with most of the actors before, but not Charlotte Rampling, who is amazing."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Oh my God. What a human being—smart, beautiful, and a great actor. I’ve just been madly in love with her. Now she calls me her not-so-secret admirer, because I love seeing her in Paris anytime. And I’d never worked with Vicky Krieps before, who’s so playful and fun, or with Mayim Bialik, but the others, yes. Luka Sabbat is an amazing guy. He was in L.A. and getting a lot of roles offered to him, and then he just said, “You know what, I don’t want to be a Black Johnny Depp. I want to DJ in Tokyo. I want to go do a fashion thing in Paris.” And he’s made his life the way he chooses. But he’s a fine actor. And Indya Moore is an actor and social activist. I worked with her in this little film I made for Saint Laurent [2021’s French Water ]. She’s a remarkable person. I loved working with her."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "One of the things that’s the same in each of these segments is that the children drive to the main location, and in the first two sections, they also drive away. There is a lot of driving in your films."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It just seems like such a common thing in our lives. I like the moments that are not dramatic. When you’re traveling between point A and B, that’s usually removed from a dramatic story. And when you have people in a car, they’re all looking forward, so they’re not noticing every little facial expression or gesture as they do when they sit across a table. Their attention is very different."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A lot of directors say that having people around a table is the hardest thing to do. That happens in the second section."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Well, yeah, you don’t have anywhere to go. I have to tell you, all of these scenes are shot in real locations. article_text:
One would have to go back to 1984’s Stranger than Paradise to find in Jim Jarmusch’s work an episodic film as funny, sad, and haunting as Father Mother Sister Brother , which won the Golden Lion at this year’s Venice Film Festival—an unusual achievement for such an understated family picture.

Father Mother Sister Brother has the delicacy and intricacy of a Mozart chamber work. Three stories, each located in a separate country, each with its own arrangement of parents and children, are connected in a large sense by the mostly ineffable complexity of filial relationships. The film opens in rural New Jersey, where a brother and sister played by Adam Driver and Mayim Bialik are visiting their loner dad—a trickster, played with barely hidden glee by Tom Waits. In the second episode, Charlotte Rampling, a Dublin-based author of popular novels prepares a very sugary high tea for her daughters—Cate Blanchett and Vicky Krieps, who are only allowed to visit her once a year. It is only in the final episode, set in Paris, that the emotions which have been dammed up to this point, break out when a pair of twentysomething twins—played by Luka Sabbat and Indya Moore—pack up childhood mementos and photographs in the apartment where they lived with their parents, who died in a mysterious plane crash.

With both metaphoric and formal connections between the three movements that delight the mind and the eye, Father Mother Sister Brother is a kind of puzzle film, where fitting the pieces together reveals a longing for a deeper resolution that may be out of reach for the characters, and is at least an open question for us.

I always think of you as making two different kinds of films: the films that have characters, relationships, and plot, and the multipart films that have just characters and relationships.

I see why you would think that. But for me, literary forms are plots. Episodic things run through literature, from The Decameron to The Canterbury Tales . [The episodic form] is used a lot in films. For me, it’s a structure that tells stories. I wrote the script for Father Mother Sister Brother in three weeks, but like with all my scripts, I had been gathering random things that just come to me with no structure. I did that for eight or nine months. With some films, it was years of gathering. And I always start with characters and write for specific actors. I write just one script and use it to get financing. But I don’t like scripts, so I don’t labor over draft after draft. The second draft of the script is what we shoot, and the next draft is what we edit. The final cut is just the final draft. With Father Mother , the first draft was just about writing dialogue for the actors I’d chosen. It’s quite a minimal thing—just sort of intimate, quiet interactions. The film has no drama, really. It has no action, it has no violence, it has no sex, it’s got nothing.

You could never separate the stories in this film, because they accumulate. And for me, the Paris one, “Sister Brother,” is a bit emotional, but it would not be if you just looked at it alone. Father Mother Sister Brother is very minimal and very observational, but it would destroy the [overall] work to show the parts separately as short films. I used flower arrangements as a metaphor in all three sections. It’s very delicate, and it required a lot of focus in shooting it, believe it or not. It’s a lot easier to shoot zombies coming out of the ground and running after people than to be aware of someone’s eyelids and the gestures of their finger and the tone of their voice and when they look away—all of that was very, very careful. It was very focused.

There are many repetitions from section to section: the flowers, something maroon, and toward the end of each section, a character looks out of a window or a door. And in the last section, the brother and sister walk into the light.

And there are car drives in each. And skateboarders. And references to toasting with various drinks—tea, water. There are water references in my last few films. There are little jokes that kind of recur as well. I was trying to build another kind of accumulation emotionally. My films are not supposed to say anything, and there’s no message. I’m not trying to make an emotional film, but, you know, it involves delicate relationships between people, and so the idea of feelings exchanged and observed is the heart of the whole film. For me.

Have you ever had parent-and-children relationships in any of your films before this?

In my first film, Permanent Vacation (1980), [the protagonist] goes to visit his mother, who’s institutionalized. Let’s see— Stranger Than Paradise , they’re cousins? Mystery Train (1989), no… I guess not, really. I kind of ran away from home when I was 17, and the family thing hasn’t really been a huge presence in my work—not the parental part, anyway.

But you are a parent. Did being a parent to a child who is now a young adult come into your writing of this?

Not in any conscious way. And again, I try not to be conscious of connections to myself. Obviously, they’re in there, but they’re for someone else to analyze or not.

The parent-child relationships are the center of each episode. And you see that the reason the children are the way they are has to do with the parent, even when the two siblings in each episode are very different from each other.

Yeah, because that’s part of being in a family. You see that the parents affected their children very clearly, but it’s not judgmental. It’s observational. We live in this fucking world now where empathy is supposed to be a weakness, right? So for me, I hope there’s something empathetic in everything I do. And this one is certainly not judging the parents. Charlotte Rampling’s mother has all these deliberate boundaries, one of them suggested by her therapist: that she just see her daughters once a year. And you definitely see the effects. And the third story is about absence and loss. The parents are gone. There’s a kind of grief in that, and that’s something you can’t change when your parents are not there anymore in your life.

Those intimate or familial relationships are almost never believable in movies. But here the relationships feel real in the little things the characters do, the way they look at each other, and the way each seems to know how the other person is going to react.

For example, when the father in the first part fails to remember that his son is divorced, the sister catches him, she cues him, and he picks it up right away. Those are the tiny things. The timing of them is very delicate, but the whole film felt like that for me. I would go back to the hotel or whatever pretty exhausted from focusing on people’s eyelashes.

How many weeks did you shoot? And did the shooting time vary for each section?

We had about 10 days to shoot each section, and some prep time. I had incredible collaborators: Fred Elmes [cinematographer] and Mark Friedberg [production designer] for the first section in New Jersey, and Yorick Le Saux to shoot the second part in Ireland and the third part in Paris. I love working with Yorick. He’s going to shoot my next film, which is all in Paris. And Marco Bittner Rosser production-designed the French and Irish sections. He did Only Lovers Left Alive (2013).

You say you write for specific actors, but how do you rehearse with them? Do you talk to them about their characters first? Because some people in this film are doing really specific character work.

For example, Mayim Bialik—I wrote it for her and Adam to be brother and sister. I didn’t know Mayim, and I do not know the TV shows she’s famous for. But I’m a Jeopardy! fan, and she was my favorite host on the show, so it was while watching her on Jeopardy! that I imagined her as Adam Driver’s sister.

I don’t really rehearse. I never rehearse a scene that will be in the film, because acting is about reacting, and I don’t want to act it out in advance. Sometimes I make up scenes on the spot and have the actors be in character, or I talk with them separately about their characters. I don’t like talking to them as though the scene means the same for everyone. They’re all different. They have different strengths.

After our first day of shooting with Tom, Adam, and Mayim, Tom took me aside and said, “So, Jim, you hired these two professional killers. What am I supposed to do?” And I told him just to do it his way. I know that they prefer to be tighter on the script, but Tom needs a longer leash. I just find the strengths of each actor. Vicky Krieps has a much different procedure than Cate Blanchett. But I love actors, and I love playing with them. They’re like children in a good way, in that they are pretending to be people on command, and their own emotions and experiences are their tools.

You have worked with most of the actors before, but not Charlotte Rampling, who is amazing.

Oh my God. What a human being—smart, beautiful, and a great actor. I’ve just been madly in love with her. Now she calls me her not-so-secret admirer, because I love seeing her in Paris anytime. And I’d never worked with Vicky Krieps before, who’s so playful and fun, or with Mayim Bialik, but the others, yes. Luka Sabbat is an amazing guy. He was in L.A. and getting a lot of roles offered to him, and then he just said, “You know what, I don’t want to be a Black Johnny Depp. I want to DJ in Tokyo. I want to go do a fashion thing in Paris.” And he’s made his life the way he chooses. But he’s a fine actor. And Indya Moore is an actor and social activist. I worked with her in this little film I made for Saint Laurent [2021’s French Water ]. She’s a remarkable person. I loved working with her.

One of the things that’s the same in each of these segments is that the children drive to the main location, and in the first two sections, they also drive away. There is a lot of driving in your films.

It just seems like such a common thing in our lives. I like the moments that are not dramatic. When you’re traveling between point A and B, that’s usually removed from a dramatic story. And when you have people in a car, they’re all looking forward, so they’re not noticing every little facial expression or gesture as they do when they sit across a table. Their attention is very different.

A lot of directors say that having people around a table is the hardest thing to do. That happens in the second section.

Well, yeah, you don’t have anywhere to go. I have to tell you, all of these scenes are shot in real locations. We’re not on stages. The house that “Father” is shot in is one very small room. The only thing I have, and it came with the location, is the chair that swivels and looks out onto that lake, which is very important, because it’s like having a time-out. I don’t know about your past, but when one is with one’s family, one needs a fucking break now and then, right?

So the time-out in the second part is the overhead shots of the table?

I go overhead also to elide time, because I can’t cut to another scene specifically. When Affonso Gonçalves, the editor that I love, went through all the footage we shot, he first cut together all the dialogue like for a TV show. And the whole thing only lasted four minutes. But the characters are supposed to be together for two hours, so we needed breaks and pauses. I wanted to change the music of it. The pauses are as important as the dialogue, or even more so for me. That was also a very small room, so I designed it to have singles on each of them and then three different two-shots. The coverage was minimal, but very carefully planned.

Could we talk a bit about deception in the film? The parents aren’t really truthful with their children and vice versa.

Yes, but I don’t think of them as evil deceptions. The Tom Waits character isn’t a nasty person, but probably he’s a terrible father. I’m not judging them. They all act these roles that supply some emotional need. It brings me back to this world we live in where there are people who are evil liars, because they lie to avoid being empathetic and to manipulate other people. But these people, they’re not evil. If they’re deceptive—families are complicated that way.

article_text:
My father, Terry Lee, who has died aged 93, was an art lecturer at Sheffield College of Art in South Yorkshire for almost three decades, and a well-regarded painter for more than half a century.

In his early years he was associated with the “Kitchen Sink” painters , who portrayed ordinary people in scenes of everyday life. But as his work evolved it became more figurative, lyrical and contemplative, and was influenced by landscape, music and literature.

Terry’s early success came with inclusion in John Berger’s Looking Forward exhibition in 1956 and prize-winning entries in successive John Moores exhibitions, but the creative energy to paint continued across five decades as he produced successive collections of work and exhibited at a series of London galleries, including the New Art Centre, Agnew’s and the Piccadilly Gallery during the 1960s and 70s.

In the 80s he was included in the British Art Show, curated by the critic William Packer, and a series of exhibitions in Maastricht in the Netherlands. A retrospective exhibition of his work was held at the Wildenstein Gallery in London in 1992.

Terry was born in Sheffield to George, a draughtsman for Firth Brown Steels, and Phylis (nee Senior), a housewife. He went to King Edward VII school and began his creative life at Sheffield College of Art in 1953, progressing to the Slade School of Art in 1955, after which he taught at his old college from 1958 until he took early retirement in 1986.

At the Slade School of Art, Terry had met fellow Sheffield artist Rosie Peters. They married in London in 1956 before returning to Sheffield, eventually settling in a dilapidated farmhouse at Calton Houses near Chatsworth in Derbyshire. There they raised four sons and worked on their art.

Beyond painting Terry loved the hills. He was a rock climber, and an early series of abstract paintings reflected this, taking inspiration from Heinrich Harrer’s book The White Spider, detailing early attempts to climb the Eiger’s infamous north face. Terry passed this passion on to his sons, whom he took on climbing trips to local Derbyshire crags and farther afield to north Wales and the Dolomites.

His marriage to Rosie ended in separation in the mid-70s; afterwards he met the artist Pamela Firth, and they married in 1998. The last chapter of his life was lived out in the mountainous beauty and solitude of Spain’s Costa Blanca, where both he and Pam continued to paint, taking inspiration from a landscape full of light.

Terry is survived by Pam and three sons, Daniel, Dominic and me, from his first marriage. His fourth and eldest son, Adam, predeceased him.

editorial_excerpt_zh: 安妮·海瑟薇与乔什·哈奈特联袂主演这部缺乏说服力的悬疑片，讲述了一位艰难求生的作家受邀为畅销书作家代笔的故事。全国上下都在呼吁一部真正好看的情色悬疑惊悚片，这种口味至少和……一样强烈。

Housemaid）的成功就证明了这一点。我们渴望与一位英俊却可能存在问题的温柔丈夫有一场性感邂逅；我们期盼着一位饱受创伤又充满危险的美丽妻子；我们渴望代入一个脆弱却勇敢的年轻人，她发现自己陷入了他们那毛骨悚然的情境中；我们还渴望在一家宏伟现代主义风格的幽静湖畔豪华别墅里度过一段时间，我们可以颤巍巍地踮着脚尖走过它那夜色中的走廊。于是，这里有一部由编剧尼克·安托斯卡（Nick Antosca）改编自科琳·霍夫弗（Colleen Hoover）小说的剧情片，片中有人进行了如此令人兴奋的越轨性爱，以至于在床头上留下了齿痕。在观看这部电影的过程中，观众可能会在自己面前的座椅靠背上留下齿痕。或者在某人的脑后。但绝不是以一种好的方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "达科塔·约翰逊（Dakota Palma）的影子，预示着会有不错的观影体验。但我们有理由怀疑，为什么罗温不向任何人——哪怕随便什么人——打听维丽蒂到底是怎么落入这般悲惨境地的。或许她本可以试着去问问那个阴险的护士（伊琳娜·德沃罗文科饰），但这个角色很快就莫名其妙地消失了。在经历了一个轰动的开场序列后，电影逐渐走向松散，第三幕完全瓦解成了一堆缺乏说服力的小型不合格情节。叙事结构似乎依赖于罗温发现的不是一份而是两份手稿，最后，我们被要求接受一种拙劣而未解的处境，将其视为什么引人入胜的暧昧。这本需要重新写一版初稿。",
