article_text:
T he nation is crying out for a really enjoyable erotic mystery-thriller, a taste potentially at least as strong as the cosy-crime fetish currently dominating our every waking moment. The success of Paul Feig’s naughty-but-not-nice movie The Housemaid proves it. We are thirsting for a sexy encounter with a dishy yet maybe problematic nice-guy husband; we are pining for a damaged and dangerous beautiful wife; we are longing to identify with a vulnerable yet gutsy young person who finds herself in the middle of their creepy scenario and we are yearning to spend some time in a secluded luxury lakeside villa of gigantic modernist proportions down whose night-time corridors we can tremblingly tiptoe. So here is a drama, adapted by screenwriter Nick Antosca from the novel by Colleen Hoover, in which someone has such excitingly transgressive sex that they leave teeth marks on the headboard. During this film, audiences may be leaving teeth marks in the seatback in front of them. Or the back of someone’s head. But not in a good way.

Dakota Johnson goes back into “Fifty Shades” ingenue-cute territory as Lowen, a struggling writer mysteriously approached by a legal team working for Verity Crawford, played by Anne Hathaway, a mega-bestselling author whose recent indisposition means that she is unable to finish her hugely lucrative novel series. Crawford’s people ask Lowen if she might be willing, in exchange for several shedloads of money, secretly to ghostwrite the rest of Crawford’s darkly saucy page-turners. Lowen agrees, largely because she is strangely drawn to Verity’s handsome, sensitive husband Jeremy, played by Josh Hartnett. She has to go and stay in their gorgeous Vermont home where she is upset to find that Verity is now immobile, using a wheelchair, and cannot speak. And she is even more upset to discover a certain manuscript by Verity which hints at a terrifying situation of which the world has no clue.

So far, so silly and so entertaining, surely? There are cheeky hints of Daphne du Maurier and Brian De Palma that promise a good time. But we are entitled to wonder why Lowen doesn’t ask someone, anyone, how exactly Verity came to be in this unhappy situation. Perhaps she might be tempted to ask the sinister nurse (Irina Dvorovenko) but this character soon simply and bafflingly disappears. After a sensational opening sequence, the film gradually unwinds, and the entirety of the third act disintegrates into a shower of small substandard plot points that don’t convince. The narrative structure seems to rest on Lowen finding not one but two manuscripts, and we are finally asked to accept a lamely unresolved situation as something fascinatingly ambiguous. This needed a new draft.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Script platform Stage 32 has launched an official marketplace to partly help combat an influx of AI-written projects.

The Stage 32 Marketplace, which launched yesterday, allows executives to discover film and TV projects that have been fully vetted via an “evaluation process” conducted by humans. Only scripts submitted across Stage 32’s 15-year existence with “exceptional valuations” will appear on the markteplace and execs can then review each project’s credentials and download scripts and materials, while requesting meetings with the creators.

Since 2011 launch, Stage 32 has evaluated 235,000 projects, it said. The marketplace kickstarts with more than 4,000 and access for 3,000 industry execs.

'Wildwood' Director Hopes People "See The Danger" In GenAI, Calls It "Antithetical" To Laika's Work

Recent projects to have started life on Stage 32 include Jeffrey Dean Morgan and Jack Quaid thriller Neighborhood Watch and No Address starrring William Baldwin.

Watch on Deadline

Richard Botto, who runs Stage 32, said the platform has a strict no AI policy and is using the marketplace as one way to combat AI slop.

“There’s no shortage of great material being written, but producers and executives simply don’t have the time or resources to evaluate everything that’s out there,” said Botto, a WGA screenwriter, producer of the Sundance award-winning Another Happy Day .

“As a writer and producer myself, I saw this challenge from both sides. I built Stage 32 to bring the industry closer together, and the Marketplace is the culmination of that vision.”

article_text:
Maha Harada Talks “In My Father’s Room”, Mark Rothko, The Book of Tea and Communicating Without Words

Maha Harada discusses “In My Father’s Room”, Mark Rothko, Japanese museums and how poems and objects can communicate without words.

After establishing herself as one of Japan’s most successful novelists, Maha Harada moved behind the camera for “In My Father’s Room”, adapting her own short story “An Unnecessary Man” into her first feature as a director. The film brings together many of the interests that have shaped her career outside cinema as well, particularly museums, visual art, Japanese aesthetics and the ways people communicate through objects rather than direct conversation. Speaking with Asian Movie Pulse, Harada discussed the transition from literature to filmmaking, the influence of Kakuzo Okakura and Mark Rothko, her own experience as a curator, the casting of Issey Ogata and Eri Watanabe, and why silence can sometimes carry more weight than words.

In My Father’s Room is screening at Busan International Film Festival

Moving from writing to directing did not feel as unnatural as might be expected. Harada explains that when she writes fiction, she already visualizes scenes very clearly, almost as though there were a camera operating inside her mind. Landscapes, rooms and movements appear to her while she works on the page, meaning that directing became another way of realizing something she had already been doing imaginatively for years.

The decision to adapt “An Unnecessary Man” also has a history stretching back around 15 years. After the story was included in Japanese high-school textbooks, Harada received a letter from a student who told her that the final scene had felt as though she were watching a movie. That response stayed with the author. It was the moment when she began seriously imagining the story as cinema, while also feeling that if it ever became a film, she wanted not simply to hand it over to someone else but to become involved herself, potentially as director. museum interview

Kakuzo Okakura’s “The Book of Tea” became one of the major philosophical foundations of both the original story and the film. Harada is particularly interested in Okakura as someone who belonged to the Meiji period yet spent substantial time outside Japan, eventually working in the United States. What matters to her is the perspective this gave him: the ability to look back at Japanese culture from outside rather than simply experiencing it from within.

That perspective also connects with Harada’s hopes for the film itself. From the beginning, she wanted “In My Father’s Room” to reach audiences outside Japan. After screenings in San Sebastian and Busan, she was encouraged by the way viewers from very different cultural backgrounds responded to the film’s attention to small things. Whether the object is a person, an artwork or something seemingly insignificant, Harada believes concentrating deeply on a small detail reflects a particular sensibility that international audiences were nevertheless able to recognize and appreciate.

Check review of the film

Mark Rothko became the other major artistic presence in the film. Harada’s interest in his paintings predates the project considerably, going back to her years working as a curator. She points out that Japanese collections acquired significant Rothko works decades ago, before the enormous prices currently associated with the artist became standard. For Harada, the fact that Japanese curators recognized the importance of his work at that point remains a source of pride. museum interview

What interests her most, however, is not the market value of Rothko’s paintings but their spirituality. She feels there is something in his work that connects naturally with the spirit of the Japanese way of tea. These two apparently distant cultural traditions therefore became parallel motifs within “In My Father’s Room”: Rothko’s abstract painting on one side and chanoyu on the other, both creating spaces where contemplation and emotion can exist without requiring conventional explanation. museum interview

Harada’s own curatorial background also informs the protagonist considerably. She acknowledges that there are many similarities between her experiences and those of the central character, particularly in relation to museum work. This naturally led the conversation toward the current position of cultural institutions in Japan, which Harada views with concern. She points to financial difficulties surrounding museum acquisitions and feels governmental cultural policy in Japan remains behind that of a number of other countries in the level of support it provides to art and cultural activity.

Casting, meanwhile, was a collaborative process between Harada and her producers. Although she had performers in mind, the final decisions emerged through discussion rather than from a completely predetermined list. Her enthusiasm for the resulting cast is particularly evident, describing the lead performance in exceptionally strong terms and emphasizing how completely the actors came to embody people she had originally created on the page.

Issey Ogata’s casting ultimately affected the screenplay itself. Once he had been confirmed as Yuichi, Harada rewrote parts of the script specifically while imagining him performing them, including the tea-related gestures and scenes. His interpretation went beyond what she had initially imagined for the character to such an extent that she now finds it difficult to imagine anyone else inhabiting the role.

Eri Watanabe, by contrast, had been one of Harada’s principal choices from much earlier in the process. The contrast between her character and Ogata’s was particularly important. Harada describes the two as fundamentally different personalities, almost opposites in temperament and in the way they approach life, yet ultimately capable of being connected through something they both recognize as beautiful.

That point of connection is poetry. A poem Yuichi writes becomes something capable of surviving beyond their failed marriage and even beyond his death. For Harada, this is one of the film’s central ideas: communication does not necessarily depend on constant conversation. Japanese culture, as she describes it, often places importance on what remains unsaid, with feelings conveyed through gestures, objects or something created and given to another person.

The poem therefore matters precisely because it lasts. Even after the relationship has ended and years have passed, the words remain in Shuko’s memory. Harada connects this again with the way of tea, where meaning can be transmitted without extensive explanation. A single object or gesture can preserve an emotional connection far longer than a conversation that disappears the moment it ends. museum interview

This philosophy ultimately explains much of “In My Father’s Room”. The movie is built around the things people leave behind: paintings, poems, memories, rooms and objects that gradually communicate what characters were unable or unwilling to say directly. Harada’s literary and curatorial backgrounds consequently do not function merely as decoration around the narrative. They provide the way in which the film itself understands human relationships.

Harada has not yet decided what her next directing project will be, although the international response to “In My Father’s Room” has made her increasingly aware of expectations surrounding another film. She is clear that she would like to direct again and hopes to bring that future work back to festivals such as Busan before presenting it to audiences elsewhere. One thing, however, already seems certain: her next film would once again be based on one of her own literary works.

For a first-time director, “In My Father’s Room” therefore represents less a sudden departure from Maha Harada’s previous career than the continuation of ideas she has been exploring through literature and museums for years. Cinema simply gives her another space in which to consider beauty, memory and the connections between people—and another way to demonstrate that sometimes the most important things are communicated precisely when nobody is speaking.

"然而,她最感兴趣的是罗特科的绘画的市场价值,而不是他们的精神性,她觉得他的作品中有与日本茶道的精神自然联系的东西,这两种显然遥远的文化传统因此在“在我父亲的房间里”中成为平行动机:罗特科的抽象绘画一边,另一边是可口可乐,两方面创造了观察和情感可以存在的空间,而不需要传统的解释。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "哈拉达的独自的巡逻背景也非常了解主角,她承认,她的经历和中心人物之间有很多相似之处,尤其是与博物馆工作有关,这自然导致了对话,朝着文化机构在日本的现状,哈拉达看起来很关心,她指出围绕博物馆收购的财务困难,并觉得日本的政府文化政策仍然落后于一些其他国家的支持水平,它为艺术和文化活动提供。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在此期间,演出是哈拉达和她的制作人之间的合作过程,尽管她有表演者在脑海中,最终的决定是通过讨论而不是从一个完全预定的列表中出现的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Issey Ogata的演出最终影响了剧本本身,一旦他被确认为Yuichi,哈拉达具体重新编写了剧本的部分,同时想象他执行它们,包括茶相关的动作和场景。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "相反,哈拉达的主要选择是从这个过程中很早就的一个,她的性格与奥加塔的对比特别重要,哈拉达描述了这两个人是根本上不同的个性,几乎在温度和他们接近生活的方式相反,但最终能够通过他们两人都认为美丽的东西连接。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这个连接点是诗歌,一首诗 Yuichi 写作成为能够超越他们失败的婚姻,甚至超越他的死亡的东西,对于哈拉达来说,这是电影的核心想法之一:沟通不一定依赖于不断的对话。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "因此,诗歌很重要,因为它持续了很长时间,即使关系结束后,几年过去了,词语仍然留在Shuko的记忆中,哈拉达再次将这与茶道联系起来,在那里意义可以传达,没有广泛的解释。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这个哲学最终解释了很多关于“在我父亲的房间里”。电影围绕着人们留下的东西构建:绘画,诗歌,记忆,房间和对象,逐渐传达了那些角色无法或不愿意直接说的话。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "哈拉达还没有决定下一个导演项目是什么,尽管国际对“在我父亲的房间”的回应使她越来越意识到周围的另一个电影的期望,她很清楚她希望再次导演,并希望将未来作品带回博桑等节日,然后在其他地方向观众展示。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“在我父亲的房间里”对于一位首次导演来说,这比玛哈哈拉达以前的职业生涯的突然离开更少,而不是她多年来一直在文学和博物馆探索的想法的延续。", "translated": true}]
excerpt_original: Maha Harada discusses “In My Father’s Room”, Mark Rothko, Japanese museums and how poems and objects can communicate without words.
translated_title_zh: 马哈·哈拉达(Maha Harada)演讲《在我父亲的房间里》(In My Father’s Room),马克·罗特科(Mark Rothko),《茶书与无言沟通》
translated_excerpt_zh: 哈拉达讲述了“在我父亲的房间里”,马克·罗特科,日本博物馆以及诗歌和物品如何在没有词语的情况下沟通。

title_original: Gareth Malone looks back: ‘After the Christmas No 1, I was meeting Simon Cowell, having tea with Gary Barlow and dinner with Andrew Lloyd Webber’
editorial_title_zh: 加雷思·马隆回首往事：“拿到圣诞单曲榜第一名之后，我在见西蒙·考威尔，和加里·巴洛喝茶，与安德鲁·劳埃德·韦伯共进晚餐”
editorial_excerpt_zh: 这位合唱团指挥兼电视主持人谈论了他在全男校里如何格格不入、合成器如何改变了一切，以及他“犹豫不决”的电视生涯起点。Gareth Malone于1975年出生于伦敦，是一位合唱团指挥兼广播主持人。他的职业生涯始于为…
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "加雷思·马隆1975年出生于伦敦，是一位合唱指挥和广播主持人。他的职业生涯始于为伦敦交响乐团运营青年与社区合唱团，并于2006年首次亮相电视节目《合唱团》。此后，他与莱斯特的男校学生、艾尔斯伯里的囚犯以及军事家属合唱团（Military Wives）合作创建了多个合唱团，并催生了冠军单曲《无论你在哪里》（Wherever You Are）。他和妻子及3个孩子住在伦敦。今年秋天，他的全新现场秀《跟着加雷思一起唱：电影时光》（Sing-A-Long-A-Gareth: At the Movies）正在英国各地巡演。", "links": [{"text": "Gareth Malone", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/gareth-malone"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当时我15岁，正开始建立自信，正如你从一身双层牛仔装束和姿势中所能看出的那样。这张照片应该是在我父母位于伯恩茅斯的家中的派对上拍的。当我不给客人们倒饮料时，我就会弹几首歌——看起来我弹的是降B大调，所以我猜当时我弹的正是《Hey Jude》。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在此之前的几年里，学校生活一直很艰难。在我10岁时，我们从温布尔登一个绿树成荫的好地方搬到了伯恩茅斯，在此之前，我的朋友既有女孩也有男孩。在一个新环境里上一所全男校是一次剧烈的档位切换，我很难交到朋友。这里没有什么身体上的欺凌，但这是一个持续被排挤的时期，这种孤立从中学头三年一直延续到了10年级。这件事从来没有被拿出来讨论过。学校从来没有说过“你正在被欺负。如果你和其他男孩有任何问题，来找我们谈谈”这样的话。我父母可能知道，因为我没有带任何朋友回家。相反，我学会了如何自己解决问题，那就是通过音乐和戏剧。这是我的救赎。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我感到非常幸运，学校里有音乐工作室——在商业研究和数学的海洋中，这是一个可以表达自我的地方。演奏合成器开启了我对音乐制作和全方位音乐极客风的终身热情。我们家里也有一台钢琴，我经常坐在钢琴前，花上感觉像是好几个小时的时间来制造各种声音。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我妈妈曾在Abbey Life Assurance和公务员部门工作。我爸爸在银行工作。他们都不是那种对事业特别上心的人——他们享受生活、家庭和房子，因此朋友们经常来串门。我的祖父母也非常重要。作为一个独生子长大，让我独自相处时感到非常自在，但这确实意味着我没有武装好其他男孩所具备的那种肢体词汇。当其他孩子胡闹时，我常常反应过度。“你为什么要那样跟我说话？没有人这样跟我说话。你为什么表现得这么愚蠢？不，我不想玩粗鲁的游戏，也不想去踢足球，因为那是五岁小孩干的事。”我更乐意坐下来聊聊天。所有这一切，可能就是为什么我倾向于和学校里的女孩交往——她们稍微懂事一点。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "十几岁时，我迷上了齐柏林飞艇（Led Zeppelin）和平克·弗洛伊德（Pink Floyd）。我在乐队里唱了很多歌——但我也对《亨利五世》中的Kenneth Branagh着迷不已，于是我决定去东英吉利大学（University of East Anglia）学习戏剧。我对假装成一头猪、做大量的滑稽表演和面具练习有着美好的回忆。这一切结束后，我继续前往伦敦的皇家音乐学院（Royal Academy of Music）学习音乐。对我来说，这是一次艰难的转变——我从照片中那个傲慢的、处于青春期过渡阶段的少年，转变为意识到相比于同龄人，我其实相当平庸。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "毕业后，我回到了伯恩茅斯。我一边卖冰淇淋赚钱，一边投递简历。一位朋友联系我，说他们看到普尔有一份青年工作的招聘广告，觉得我很适合。他们想要一个年轻、懂音乐的人，去和当地一处贫困程度很高的住宅区里的儿童一起工作。他们有一个小音乐室，里面有几件破烂的乐器，我会试着教他们演奏。这就是我那种把机会、安全空间和音乐带给每个人的热情的来源。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我也意识到，要让人们信任我，我必须做我自己。我来自完全不同的世界，而且我当时懵懂、天真。孩子们能闻到我身上的中产阶级气息，所以任何假装冷酷和高傲的把戏都是行不通的。我必须严格地做我自己。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我的工作是赋予他人自信，但在建立自我价值感这方面，我绝对经历了一段心路历程，尤其是面对镜头的时候。我当时正在和伦敦交响乐团合作并运营一个合唱团，这时我第一次有了上电视的机会。《The Choir》的制作人看到我们的谷歌评分很高，于是联系了我们。节目内容是在米德尔塞克斯的诺斯霍特高中（Northolt high school）组建一个合唱团，在整个过程中，我试图将在青年小组学到的真实方法应用到镜头前。我得到了这份从未做过的高难度工作，但我是在全国电视观众面前边学边干的。我一直在被拍摄。导演说：“我想要你生气时的样子，我想要你心烦时的样子，我想要你开心时的样子。我不会让你看起来像个傻子。”他信守了诺言，但我记得当时我很紧张，试图显得胸有成竹，而且相当犹豫不决。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在时事通讯推广之后", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当你被认出来时，这可能是一份厚礼，但当你倒垃圾时，它也可能是一种负担。当《军事家属合唱团》登上排行榜第1名时，我突然被抛入了新的名气层级：我在见西蒙·考威尔，和加里·巴洛喝茶，与安德鲁·劳埃德·韦伯共进晚餐。我对那个时期的记忆是它非常浓烈——当你拿下圣诞单曲榜第1名时，就像是加入了一个奇怪的俱乐部，里面有来自斯雷德乐队（Slade）的诺迪（Noddy）和沙金·斯蒂文斯（Shakin’ Stevens）这样的人。然而，所有的浮华与喧嚣从未让我偏离20年前我涉足这个行业初衷：专注于我对音乐的热情以及艺术在人们生活中的重要性。音乐和在合唱团中唱歌有一种极其治愈的力量。当人们聚在一起时，他们会从中受到鼓舞。今年年初我失去了一位朋友，在他去世前，他对我说了一些深情触动的话：“我们终究没去喝那一品脱啤酒。”这太残酷了。如此简单的一件事，却因为我们俩都全身心投入到各自的职业中而显得不可能。电视、学位——所有这些成就都非常美好。它们是我许多幸福赖以存在的基石。但这并不是最主要的。人与社区才是。", "links": [{"text": "Military Wives got to No 1", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/music/2011/dec/27/military-wives-fuel-choral-boom"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当我15岁时，我对自己的成年生活有着清晰的设想。它包含一个摆满各种乐器的音乐工作室。少年时期的我会非常高兴地知道，在我花园的尽头有一个小窝点，里面有钢琴、架子鼓、沙锤、马拉卡斯鼓、吉他、邦戈鼓、合成器、一台电脑和扬声器——没有哪一天我不在做音乐，其中一半时间是在独自琢磨，其余时间则是在和别人一起创作音乐。对于我现在练习这么多热瑜伽，他可能会感到困惑。但如果知道我依然喜欢牛仔衬衫，他一定会很高兴。", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "家庭", "links": [{"text": "Family", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/family"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Born in London in 1975, Gareth Malone is a choirmaster and broadcaster. He began his career running youth and community choirs for the London Symphony Orchestra and first appeared on TV in 2006’s The Choir. He has since created choirs with Leicester schoolboys, Aylesbury prisoners, as well as the Military Wives, which produced the No 1 single, Wherever You Are. He lives in London with his wife and three children. His new live show, Sing-A-Long-A-Gareth: At the Movies, is on tour across the UK this autumn.", "links": [{"text": "Gareth Malone", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/gareth-malone"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I was 15 and just coming into my own with my confidence , as you can tell by the double denim and the pose. The photo would have been taken at a party at my parents’ house in Bournemouth. When I wasn’t filling up guests’ drinks, I’d be playing some songs – it looks like I’m playing B flat major, so I suspect at this very moment it was Hey Jude."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For a few years prior to this, school had been difficult. We moved from a nice leafy part of Wimbledon to Bournemouth when I was 10, and until that point I had friends who were both girls and boys. Going to the all-boys grammar school in a new area was an aggressive gear shift and I struggled to make friends. There was no physical bullying, but it was a sustained period of ostracisation that went on for the first three years of secondary school and dribbled on into year 10. It wasn’t ever discussed. There was no “you’re being bullied. If you have a problem with any other boys, come and talk to us,” from the school. My parents probably knew because I wasn’t bringing any friends over. Instead I learned how to take care of my own problems, which was through music and theatre. My saving grace."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I feel so lucky that I had the music studio at school – a place to be expressive in a sea of business studies and maths. Playing the synthesisers started my lifelong passion for production and all-round music nerdery. We also had a piano at home and I used to sit at it and make sounds for what felt like hours."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Mum worked for Abbey Life Assurance and for the civil service. Dad worked for a bank. Neither of them were particularly career-minded – they enjoyed their life, their family and their house, hence friends often coming over. My grandparents were very important, too. Growing up as an only child made me very comfortable in my own company, but it did mean I wasn’t armed with some of the physical vocabulary that other boys had. I used to overreact when other kids were playing up. “Why are you speaking to me like that? No one speaks to me like that. Why are you behaving in this stupid way? No, I don’t want to play rough, or go and play football, because that’s what five-year-olds do.” I was far happier to sit and have a conversation. All of which is possibly why I gravitated towards the girls at school – they were a bit more sensible."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In my teens I got very into Led Zeppelin and Pink Floyd. I was singing a lot in bands – but I was also obsessed with Kenneth Branagh in Henry V, so I decided to study drama at University of East Anglia. I have fond memories of pretending to be a pig, and doing lots of clowning and mask work. Once that was over, I went on to study music at the Royal Academy of Music in London. It was a difficult transition for me – I went from that arrogant tweeny, liminal stage, as pictured, to realising that I was, actually, just fairly average compared with my peers."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "After graduating, I went back to Bournemouth. I was selling ice-cream to make some money while sending out CVs. A friend got in touch and said they had seen an advert for some youth work in Poole, and thought I’d be good at it. They wanted someone young and musical to work with local children who lived on an estate with a high level of deprivation. They had a little music room with a couple of ropey instruments that I would try to teach them how to play. That’s where my passion for giving everyone opportunities – a safe space and music – came from."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I also realised that to get people to trust me, I had to be myself. I was from a totally different side of the tracks and I was wide-eyed, naive. The kids could smell the middle-classness on me, so any pretending to be cool and aloof wouldn’t work. I had to be rigorously myself."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "My job is to give others confidence, but I’ve definitely gone on a journey with my own self-esteem, especially when it comes to being in front of the camera. I was working with the London Symphony Orchestra and running a choir when I first got the opportunity to be on TV. The producers of The Choir had seen that we had a high Google rating so they got in touch. The show was about starting a choir at Northolt high school in Middlesex, and throughout, I tried to apply the same method of authenticity on camera that I’d learned with the youth group. I had been given this amazing job that I’d never done before, but I was learning to do it on national television. I was being filmed constantly. The director said: “I want you when you’re angry, I want you when you’re upset, I want you when you’re happy. I won’t make you look like an idiot.” He stuck to his word, but I remember being nervous, trying to look in control, and dithering quite a lot."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "after newsletter promotion"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "When you’re recognised it can be a great gift, but a burden when you’re, say, taking out your bins. When Military Wives got to No 1 , I was suddenly thrown into a new level of celebrity: I was meeting Simon Cowell, having tea with Gary Barlow and dinner with Andrew Lloyd Webber. My memories of that time was that it was intense – when you have a Christmas No 1, it’s like you’ve joined a weird club with people like Noddy from Slade and Shakin’ Stevens. None of the bells and whistles has ever distracted me from the reason I got into this industry in the first place 20 years ago, however. Focusing on my passion for music and the importance of art in people’s lives. There’s something so healing about music, and singing in a choir. When people come together, they are buoyed up by it. I lost a friend at the beginning of this year and before he died he said something deeply touching to me: “We never did go for that pint.” It was brutal. Such a simple thing that felt impossible as we were both absorbed in our careers. The telly, the degrees – all of those achievements are wonderful. It’s the foundation upon which a lot of my happiness is at rest. But it’s not the main thing. article_text:
Born in London in 1975, Gareth Malone is a choirmaster and broadcaster. He began his career running youth and community choirs for the London Symphony Orchestra and first appeared on TV in 2006’s The Choir. He has since created choirs with Leicester schoolboys, Aylesbury prisoners, as well as the Military Wives, which produced the No 1 single, Wherever You Are. He lives in London with his wife and three children. His new live show, Sing-A-Long-A-Gareth: At the Movies, is on tour across the UK this autumn.

I was 15 and just coming into my own with my confidence , as you can tell by the double denim and the pose. The photo would have been taken at a party at my parents’ house in Bournemouth. When I wasn’t filling up guests’ drinks, I’d be playing some songs – it looks like I’m playing B flat major, so I suspect at this very moment it was Hey Jude.

For a few years prior to this, school had been difficult. We moved from a nice leafy part of Wimbledon to Bournemouth when I was 10, and until that point I had friends who were both girls and boys. Going to the all-boys grammar school in a new area was an aggressive gear shift and I struggled to make friends. There was no physical bullying, but it was a sustained period of ostracisation that went on for the first three years of secondary school and dribbled on into year 10. It wasn’t ever discussed. There was no “you’re being bullied. If you have a problem with any other boys, come and talk to us,” from the school. My parents probably knew because I wasn’t bringing any friends over. Instead I learned how to take care of my own problems, which was through music and theatre. My saving grace.

I feel so lucky that I had the music studio at school – a place to be expressive in a sea of business studies and maths. Playing the synthesisers started my lifelong passion for production and all-round music nerdery. We also had a piano at home and I used to sit at it and make sounds for what felt like hours.

Mum worked for Abbey Life Assurance and for the civil service. Dad worked for a bank. Neither of them were particularly career-minded – they enjoyed their life, their family and their house, hence friends often coming over. My grandparents were very important, too. Growing up as an only child made me very comfortable in my own company, but it did mean I wasn’t armed with some of the physical vocabulary that other boys had. I used to overreact when other kids were playing up. “Why are you speaking to me like that? No one speaks to me like that. Why are you behaving in this stupid way? No, I don’t want to play rough, or go and play football, because that’s what five-year-olds do.” I was far happier to sit and have a conversation. All of which is possibly why I gravitated towards the girls at school – they were a bit more sensible.

In my teens I got very into Led Zeppelin and Pink Floyd. I was singing a lot in bands – but I was also obsessed with Kenneth Branagh in Henry V, so I decided to study drama at University of East Anglia. I have fond memories of pretending to be a pig, and doing lots of clowning and mask work. Once that was over, I went on to study music at the Royal Academy of Music in London. It was a difficult transition for me – I went from that arrogant tweeny, liminal stage, as pictured, to realising that I was, actually, just fairly average compared with my peers.

After graduating, I went back to Bournemouth. I was selling ice-cream to make some money while sending out CVs. A friend got in touch and said they had seen an advert for some youth work in Poole, and thought I’d be good at it. They wanted someone young and musical to work with local children who lived on an estate with a high level of deprivation. They had a little music room with a couple of ropey instruments that I would try to teach them how to play. That’s where my passion for giving everyone opportunities – a safe space and music – came from.

I also realised that to get people to trust me, I had to be myself. I was from a totally different side of the tracks and I was wide-eyed, naive. The kids could smell the middle-classness on me, so any pretending to be cool and aloof wouldn’t work. I had to be rigorously myself.

My job is to give others confidence, but I’ve definitely gone on a journey with my own self-esteem, especially when it comes to being in front of the camera. I was working with the London Symphony Orchestra and running a choir when I first got the opportunity to be on TV. The producers of The Choir had seen that we had a high Google rating so they got in touch. The show was about starting a choir at Northolt high school in Middlesex, and throughout, I tried to apply the same method of authenticity on camera that I’d learned with the youth group. I had been given this amazing job that I’d never done before, but I was learning to do it on national television. I was being filmed constantly. The director said: “I want you when you’re angry, I want you when you’re upset, I want you when you’re happy. I won’t make you look like an idiot.” He stuck to his word, but I remember being nervous, trying to look in control, and dithering quite a lot.

after newsletter promotion

When you’re recognised it can be a great gift, but a burden when you’re, say, taking out your bins. When Military Wives got to No 1 , I was suddenly thrown into a new level of celebrity: I was meeting Simon Cowell, having tea with Gary Barlow and dinner with Andrew Lloyd Webber. My memories of that time was that it was intense – when you have a Christmas No 1, it’s like you’ve joined a weird club with people like Noddy from Slade and Shakin’ Stevens. None of the bells and whistles has ever distracted me from the reason I got into this industry in the first place 20 years ago, however. Focusing on my passion for music and the importance of art in people’s lives. There’s something so healing about music, and singing in a choir. When people come together, they are buoyed up by it. I lost a friend at the beginning of this year and before he died he said something deeply touching to me: “We never did go for that pint.” It was brutal. Such a simple thing that felt impossible as we were both absorbed in our careers. The telly, the degrees – all of those achievements are wonderful. It’s the foundation upon which a lot of my happiness is at rest. But it’s not the main thing. People and community are.

When I was 15 I had a clear vision of what I wanted with my adult life. It involved a music studio with lots of instruments in it. The teenage me would be overjoyed to know that at the end of my garden is a little den with a piano, drums, shakers, maracas, guitars, bongos, synthesisers, a computer and speakers – that there’s never a day when I’m not doing music, half of it tinkering alone, the rest making music with other people. He’d probably be confused about the amount of hot yoga I currently do. But glad to know I still like a denim shirt.

article_text:
In a suit filed in Los Angeles Superior Court on Wednesday, the Norton Simon Museum of Art in Pasadena, California, is arguing that it is the proper owner of 16th-century diptych that was looted by the Nazis and later sold to its founder. The heirs have been fighting for the artwork for decades, though the family chose after World War II not to sue for its return.

The museum opposes an attempt by the Jewish Federation-Council of Greater Los Angeles and its board chair Daniel Gryczman, who sued in September for the return of Lucas Cranach the Elder ’s 16th-century diptych painting Adam and Eve . Marei von Saher, heir to the Dutch dealer Jacques Goudstikker, who owned the piece before the war, has sued unsuccessfully for the paintings before, and has now transferred her rights to the federation.

In August 2016, the same court ruled after 12 years of litigation that the museum was the rightful owner. The Supreme Court declined to reopen the case. But the heirs are suing in the wake of amendments to the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery (HEAR) Act, that stipulate that US defendants in restitution conflicts may not use certain types of defenses, including statutes of limitation and the “act of state” doctrine.

The painting and other artworks owned by Goudstikker have a complicated history, as the museum’s filing puts forth. When the Soviet Union auctioned off a collection from the aristocratic Stroganoff family in 1931, Goudstikker bought the Cranach. When the Nazis invaded the Netherlands in 1940, Goudstikker left behind his gallery with some 1,200 works; he died in transit to the US in an accident on board ship. His wife Desirée inherited his company, which was forced by the Nazis to sell off its assets; Nazi Reichsmarschall Herman Göring bought the Cranach and other pieces. Allied forces recovered the works and restored them to the Netherlandish government. Desirée did not opt to petition for the return of the Cranach, not wishing to run an art dealership, but did successfully pursue restitution for other property.

In 1961, a Stroganoff heir filed for return of the Cranach and a Rembrandt, saying they had been looted by the Soviets. It was ultimately agreed in 1966 that he could buy the Cranach, which he then sold to the Norton Simon Art Foundation for $800,000. The artwork has remained on public view ever since.

Von Saher revived the business after Desirée Goudstikker died in 1996 and began fighting to get the Cranach back in 1998. The Dutch government refused, saying the matter had been rightfully resolved. In 2001, the Dutch instituted a revised policy, under which Von Saher claimed for return of some other works in 2004, but not the Cranach. The Dutch state approved the return of some artworks, while also saying the matter had been properly settled.

Von Saher sued the Norton Simon in 2007 and was denied three times, says the museum.

A representative for the Jewish Federation did not immediately answer a request for comment on the museum’s lawsuit.

解説・あらすじ

パリ・モンマルトルを舞台に空想好きな女性アメリの日常と不器用な恋の行方をポップな映像とブラックユーモアを交えて描き、フランスのみならず日本でも大ヒットを記録したロマンティックコメディ。 幼い頃から空想の世界で過ごしてきたアメリは、そのまま大人になり、モンマルトルの古いアパートに1人で暮らしながらカフェで働いている。他人とのコミュニケーションは苦手だったが、偶然発見した宝箱を持ち主に返したことをきっかけに、誰かを少しだけ幸せにすることに喜びを見出すように。そんなある日、アメリは他人の証明写真を収集する不思議な青年ニノと出会い、恋心を抱く。 オドレイ・トトゥが主人公アメリを魅力たっぷりに演じ、「クリムゾン・リバー」など監督としても活躍するマチュー・カソビッツがニノ役で共演。監督は「デリカテッセン」のジャン＝ピエール・ジュネ。2023年、ジュネ監督監修のデジタルリマスター版でリバイバル公開。2026年、日本公開25周年を記念してリバイバル公開。

2001年製作／121分／フランス 原題または英題：Le fabuleux destin d'Amélie Poulain 配給：スターキャットアルバトロス・フィルム 劇場公開日：2026年11月13日

その他の公開日：2001年11月17日（日本初公開）、2023年11月17日

さよなら、私のロシア

劇場公開日： 2026年11月14日

映画館を探す

予告編を見る

U-NEXTで 関連作品を見る PR

解説・あらすじ

祖国ロシアによるウクライナ侵攻を受けてロシア国営放送の職を辞したジャーナリストのジャンナ・アガラコワが、祖国と家族を愛するがゆえに犯した自らの過ちと悔恨、そして故郷喪失の痛みをつづったドキュメンタリー。 2022年3月、ロシア国営放送の海外特派員ジャンナ・アガラコワは、ウクライナ侵攻に抗議し辞職する。彼女は自分がいつからプロパガンダに加担していたのかの答えを求め、過去をさかのぼりはじめる。ジャンナはイタリア人の夫と思春期の娘アリーチェと3人でニューヨークに暮らしていた。3歳でロシアを離れたアリーチェにルーツを知ってもらうため、親子は休暇にあわせてロシア各地を旅するようになる。“ロシア人らしさ”を求める母の考えを理解しながらも、受け入れることも受け流すこともできないアリーチェと、ロシアを偉大で素晴らしい国だと信じ、誇りを胸に仕事をまっとうするジャンナ。広大な土地にまばらな人家、決して豊かとは言えない人々の暮らし、少しずつ濃くなっていく戦争の気配。4つの夏と1つの冬の旅を含む家族の記録には、母娘のズレとロシアのリアルが映されていた。やがてアリーチェの決定的なひと言をきっかけに、ロシアを巡る家族旅行はジャンナの内省の旅へと変貌する。 ジャンナ・アガラコワが自ら監督を務め、数百時間におよぶ映像をもとに3年の歳月をかけて完成させた。

article_text:
ちっぽけな僕の、おおきな世界

劇場公開日： 2026年11月6日

映画館を探す

予告編を見る

U-NEXTで 関連作品を見る PR

解説・あらすじ

「少年の君」のジャクソン・イーが主演を務め、脳性まひの青年が自らの意思で人生を切りひらいていく姿を、家族それぞれが抱える痛みとともに描いたヒューマンドラマ。 脳性まひを抱える20歳のリウ・チュンホーは、身体の障害や周囲の偏見、母親の身勝手な愛情に向き合いながら、自分らしい人生を模索している。祖母のスーチュンだけは「障害のある孫」ではなくひとりの青年としてチュンホーに接し、社会へ踏み出す勇気を与え続けてきた。やがて、若い女性ヤーヤとの出会いや新たな経験を通して、チュンホーの心に少しずつ変化が起こりはじめる。 ジャクソン・イーが主人公チュンホーを熱演し、中国電影金鶏賞および大衆電影百花賞で最優秀主演男優賞を獲得。破天荒な祖母スーチュンを「フェアウェル」のダイアナ・リンが演じた。「春夢」「老人」「春潮」などで高く評価されたヤン・リーナーが監督を務め、脚本を「シスター 夏のわかれ道」のヨウ・シャオイン、音楽を小林武史が担当。2024年・第37回東京国際映画祭コンペティション部門にて観客賞を受賞（映画祭上映時タイトル「小さな私」）。

article_text:
Taika Waititi’s Klara and the Sun premiered at the 70th BFI London Film Festival at BFI Southbank in London, England, and its stars came out to celebrate.

Amy Adams, Jenna Ortega, Rachel Foreman, Aran Murphy, Natasha Lyonne, and more were on the red carpet. They were also joined by Florence Pugh, Rita Ora, Taika Waititi, among many others.

Check out the red carpet gallery at the end of this piece to see all the looks from the event.

RELATED: ‘Klara And The Sun’ Review: Taika Waititi’s Latest Is A Curiously Flat Dystopian Comedy-Drama – London Film Festival

Klara and the Sun is a dystopian science fiction film set for release in theaters on October 23 via Sony Pictures Releasing. Waititi directed the film, co-wrote it with Dahvi Waller, and it’s based on Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 novel of the same name.

The film is set in a dystopian future where advances in genetic engineering have divided humans into isolated social classes; an android named Klara tries to bond with Josie, a sick girl she was purchased for.

Jenna Ortega plays Klara, Mia Tharia plays Josie, Amy Adams plays Josie’s mother, Chrissie, and Aran Murphy plays Josie’s best friend, Rick. The cast also includes Natasha Lyonne, Steve Buscemi, Rachel House, Harry Greenwood, and Sophia Bryant-Taukiri.

RELATED: ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’ Character Posters: Joseph Zada, Mckenna Grace, Maya Hawke, Glenn Close & More

David Heyman, Garrett Basch, and Waititi produced Klara and the Sun . Executive producers include Gary Barber, Alex G. Scott, Jeffrey Clifford, Rosie Alison and author Kazuo Ishiguro.

RELATED: ‘Clayface’ Red Carpet Premiere Photos: Tom Rhys Harries, Naomi Ackie & More

title_original: One in a Million Review: An Epic Saga of Exile and Assimilation
editorial_title_zh: 《百万分之一》影评：一部关于流亡与同化的史诗传奇
editorial_excerpt_zh: 注：本影评最初发布于我们2026年圣丹斯电影节报道中。影片将于10月21日全美院线上映。“战争并不是一个人能经历的最艰难的事情。它没有接下来发生的事那么难。”这几句开场白是伊塔卜·阿扎姆（Itab Azzam）与……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "注：本影评最初发布于我们2026年圣丹斯电影节报道中。影片将于10月21日全美院线上映。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“战争并不是一个人能经历的最艰难的事情。它没有接下来发生的事那么难。”这几句开场白是伊塔卜·阿扎姆（Itab Azzam）与杰克·麦金尼斯（Jack MacInnes）共同执导的纪录片《百万分之一》（One in a Million）的核心指引。这是一部关于流亡与同化的史诗传奇，聚焦于从饱受战争蹂躏、危机四伏的祖国叙利亚逃离、前往德国重新开始生活的伊斯拉（Israa）及其家人。影片历时十年拍摄，这个家庭的故事也兼具成长小说的特质，自由的喜悦与同化的喧嚣共同考验着每一位家庭成员的纽带。尽管影片的章节式结构以及考虑到其宏大视野相对紧凑的时长，导致某些细节未能得到充分挖掘，但两位导演以感人的细腻度捕捉到了：感知到的自由并不总等同于真正的独立。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "影片初次向我们介绍伊斯拉时她大约11岁，时间大约在2015年，我们见证了她一家人从叙利亚经海路到希腊、再穿过数个国家最终抵达避难所德国的惊心动魄的旅程。在他们离开之前，孩子们提到他们并不害怕死亡，同时我们看到了令人难忘的画面：幼小的幼儿们穿上了橙色救生衣。但在航行过程中，两个孩子因严寒不幸夭折，这让原本活泼开朗、性格受到震动的伊斯拉留下了创伤。随着影片进行到不到三分之一时他们终于抵达德国，接下来的旅程不再是物理距离的跨越，而是情感上的重重障碍，因为随后的十年同化深深影响了他们家庭单元的方方面面。《百万分之一》展现了全新的视角：我们开始听到更多来自伊斯拉的父亲塔里克（Tarek），以及最终来自她的母亲尼斯林（Nisreen）的心声，此时坚守叙利亚传统的矛盾情感开始与流行文化、成长和浪漫发生冲突。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "正如我们从随性拍摄的镜头以及每隔几年进行一次的回访式摆拍采访场所能看到的那样，阿扎姆和麦金尼斯与他们的拍摄对象显然关系密切，这带来了一层额外的情感深度：伊斯拉的烦恼从纯粹的生存转变为树立自己的个性，摆脱她那控制欲强的父亲。虽然某些重大生活事件最好由观众亲自去体验，但父亲与女儿之间以及丈夫与妻子之间的这种冲突，随着在一个允许这种改变的国家中形成新的身份，以一种令人心碎又获得解放的方式展开。由于某些时间跨度相当巨大，即使他们相互交织的欲望之间的脉络很容易连接起来，拍摄对象的人生轨迹和情感有时仍会给人一种拼凑感。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "导演们还触及了这个世界奇异而悲伤的本质，因为塔里克再次见证了极右翼的压迫。德国选择党（AfD）涌入德国，呼吁大规模驱逐移民，但与在叙利亚不同的是，塔里克能够自豪地站在抗议者中间，而不必担心受到伤害。这给人一种感觉：世界上没有哪个角落能真正对所有人敞开怀抱，但至少有些国家仍在尽最大努力展现善意。这种对政治和社会自由的渴望与无法在自家屋檐下享有个人自主权之间的悖论，成为了影片的核心线索，并伴随着离开一个你多年来称之为祖国的国家的精神痛苦。塔里克是其家人难以言喻的痛苦之源，但导演们很好地探讨了这种折磨背后的原因。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尽管不到100分钟的时长不足以捕捉长达10年、涉及多位拍摄对象的每个细微差别，《百万分之一》依然是一部雄心勃勃、感人至深的宣言，它表明只有当个人独立得以实现时，完整的自由感才会到来。许多纪录片——即使是杰出的纪录片——往往将镜头聚焦于难民经历中某个特定窗口的狭隘视角，而阿扎姆与麦金尼斯的这部纪录片则认为，找到庇护所仅仅是通往获得自由的复杂内心情感的第1步。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《百万分之一》在2026年圣丹斯电影节上首映。", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Note: This review was originally published as part of our 2026 Sundance coverage. The film opens in theaters on October 21."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“War is not the hardest thing a person can go through. It’s not as hard as what comes after.” These opening words are the guiding theme of Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes’ One in a Million , an epic saga of exile and assimilation centered on Israa and her family, Syrian refugees who flee their perilous, war-torn homeland to restart life in Germany. Filmed over a decade, the family story also doubles as a coming-of-age tale where both the joy of freedom and tumult of assimilation test every family member’s bonds. While the film’s episodic structure and, considering its sprawling canvas, relatively succinct runtime leave some details less explored, the filmmakers capture, with moving sensitivity, how perceived liberty doesn’t always mean true independence."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "We’re first introduced to Israa at age 11, circa 2015, and witness her family’s harrowing journey by sea from Syria to Greece, then through multiple countries to the ultimate haven of Germany. Before they leave, children note how they are not scared to die while we see the unforgettable image of small toddlers putting on orange life vests. But during the voyage, two kids succumb to the cold, traumatizing Israa as her normally bubbly personality is shaken. Eventually arriving in Germany less than a third into the film, the rest of the journey is not one of physical distance but emotional obstacles, as the next ten years of assimilation deeply affect every fabric of their family unit. One in a Million opens to new perspectives: we start hearing more from Israa’s father Tarek and, eventually, her mother Nisreen as conflicted feelings of adhering to Syrian tradition start clashing with popular culture, growing up, and romance."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "As we can see both in off-the-cuff footage and staged interviews checking in every few years, Azzam and MacInnes are clearly close with their subjects, leading to another emotional layer when Israa’s woes go from pure survival to establishing her own personality, one free from her controlling father. While certain major life events are best left experienced, this conflict between both father and daughter as well as husband and wife plays out in heartbreaking, liberating ways as new identities are formed in a country allowing such change. Because certain time leaps are so substantial, the arcs and feelings of the subjects can feel patchwork even if the dots of their warring desires are easily connected."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The filmmakers also touch on the strange, sad nature of the world as Tarek witnesses, once again, far-right oppression. The AfD descends on Germany, calling for the mass deportation of immigrants, but unlike in Syria, Tarek is able to proudly stand along the protestors without fear of getting harmed. article_text:
Note: This review was originally published as part of our 2026 Sundance coverage. The film opens in theaters on October 21.

“War is not the hardest thing a person can go through. It’s not as hard as what comes after.” These opening words are the guiding theme of Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes’ One in a Million , an epic saga of exile and assimilation centered on Israa and her family, Syrian refugees who flee their perilous, war-torn homeland to restart life in Germany. Filmed over a decade, the family story also doubles as a coming-of-age tale where both the joy of freedom and tumult of assimilation test every family member’s bonds. While the film’s episodic structure and, considering its sprawling canvas, relatively succinct runtime leave some details less explored, the filmmakers capture, with moving sensitivity, how perceived liberty doesn’t always mean true independence.

We’re first introduced to Israa at age 11, circa 2015, and witness her family’s harrowing journey by sea from Syria to Greece, then through multiple countries to the ultimate haven of Germany. Before they leave, children note how they are not scared to die while we see the unforgettable image of small toddlers putting on orange life vests. But during the voyage, two kids succumb to the cold, traumatizing Israa as her normally bubbly personality is shaken. Eventually arriving in Germany less than a third into the film, the rest of the journey is not one of physical distance but emotional obstacles, as the next ten years of assimilation deeply affect every fabric of their family unit. One in a Million opens to new perspectives: we start hearing more from Israa’s father Tarek and, eventually, her mother Nisreen as conflicted feelings of adhering to Syrian tradition start clashing with popular culture, growing up, and romance.

As we can see both in off-the-cuff footage and staged interviews checking in every few years, Azzam and MacInnes are clearly close with their subjects, leading to another emotional layer when Israa’s woes go from pure survival to establishing her own personality, one free from her controlling father. While certain major life events are best left experienced, this conflict between both father and daughter as well as husband and wife plays out in heartbreaking, liberating ways as new identities are formed in a country allowing such change. Because certain time leaps are so substantial, the arcs and feelings of the subjects can feel patchwork even if the dots of their warring desires are easily connected.

The filmmakers also touch on the strange, sad nature of the world as Tarek witnesses, once again, far-right oppression. The AfD descends on Germany, calling for the mass deportation of immigrants, but unlike in Syria, Tarek is able to proudly stand along the protestors without fear of getting harmed. There’s the sense that no corner of the world will ever truly be welcoming to all, but at least some countries still put their best foot forward. This paradox between desiring political and social freedom but not allowing personal autonomy under your own roof becomes a central thread, coupled with the mental anguish of leaving a country you called home for so many years. Tarek is the source of unspeakable pain to his family, but the filmmakers do well to touch on the reasons for such torment.

Although just under 100 minutes isn’t enough time to capture every nuance of 10 years with multiple subjects, One in a Million is an ambitious, affecting declaration that a complete sense of freedom will only arrive when personal independence is fulfilled. With many documentaries, even great ones, taking a narrow view of a specific window of the refugee experience, Azzam and MacInnes’ documentary contends that finding asylum is only the first step in a complex internal struggle to be free.

One in a Million premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival.
